 ## 6. Viewing-to-program matching design
+
+### Exact rule and double-count prevention
+
+For view interval `V=[v_start,v_stop)` and airing `A=[a_start,a_start+duration)` on the same channel:
+
+```text
+vsetv_id == channel_id
+overlap_seconds = max(0, min(v_stop, a_end) - max(v_start, a_start))
+```
+
+Use half-open intervals: touching endpoints have zero overlap. All interval arithmetic should use UTC elapsed seconds under the documented local-clock interpretation. Merely joining on channel/date or choosing the first broadcast after a view starts is incorrect.
+
+Proposed processing order:
+
+1. Read exact string user IDs; parse both timestamp formats explicitly; check/record the timezone assumption. Reject/quarantine invalid spans without editing originals.
+2. Establish training/validation boundaries before any behavior aggregation. Clip viewing time to its period. The 1,007 raw intervals crossing the training cutoff contribute only their pre-cutoff portion to training; remaining time is validation evidence only.
+3. Deduplicate schedule airing identity `(channel_id, start_utc, end_utc, tv_show_id)` after comparing metadata; preserve conflict diagnostics. Boundary spillovers from the adjacent historical file can complete availability, but not expand behavior cutoffs.
+4. Group view fragments by `(user_id, channel_id)` within the period, union overlapping/touching fragments, then intersect with all eligible labelled airings. This avoids duplicate-time credit while allowing one long session to match multiple programs.
+5. Accumulate disjoint overlap pieces for each `(user_id, channel, airing_start, airing_end, tv_show_id, period)` before applying the watched threshold. Two short fragments of the same airing can jointly qualify. Do not add separate repeat broadcasts merely to pass a per-airing threshold.
+6. Count qualifying distinct airings for frequency, retain union seconds as an optional weight, and deduplicate `(user_id, program_id)` for binary relevance/support. Check total credited time per user-airing does not exceed its broadcast duration. If overlapping different labelled IDs exist on one channel, quarantine ambiguous time or resolve it explicitly and identically for all methods; historical diagnostics did not encounter this on viewed channels.
+
+Avoid a Cartesian DataFrame join. Channel-sorted interval sweeps or start-time/prefix-max-end indexes plus bounded search are feasible. The inspection used SQLite ordering and per-channel interval indexes, not an exported interaction training set.

 ## 7. MAP@5 definition
+
+**Confirmed from the exam:** metric is MAP@K, higher is better, and this exam fixes K=5. **Confirmed from presentation pp.4–5:** normalize each user's AP by `min(K, |R_u|)`, then macro-average across users. The slides explicitly say to match the evaluator convention. The detailed live Kaggle scorer implementation was not retrievable, so empty-label/duplicate-prediction behavior and hidden relevance construction remain unconfirmed by the platform.
+
+For the proposed local protocol, let `R_u` be the set of distinct positive program IDs with a qualifying validation airing, and `p_u[1:5]` the ordered predictions. Define `hit_u(r)=1` only for a relevant ID's first appearance; otherwise 0. Then:
+
+```text
+P_u@r  = (sum_{j=1..r} hit_u(j)) / r
+AP_u@5 = (sum_{r=1..5} P_u@r * hit_u(r)) / min(5, |R_u|), when |R_u| > 0
+MAP@5  = (1 / |U|) * sum_{u in U} AP_u@5
+```
+
+**Proposed edge policies:** empty `R_u` gives AP=0 for the primary all-user metric; duplicate predicted IDs cannot earn repeated hits and are rejected by the output validator; exactly five unique positive eligible IDs are required. Macro-average users, not views, and do not divide by the number of retrieved hits or by five when fewer than five relevant items exist.
+
+The presentation's example is a useful future unit-test target: relevant `{A,B,C}`, ranking `A,B,D,C,E` gives `(1+1+3/4)/3 = 11/12`; `D,A,E,B,C` gives `(1/2+2/4+3/5)/3 = 8/15`. These are illustrative arithmetic examples, **not project experiment results or student personal verification**.
+
+The slide's competition screenshot describes “five most preferred” programs from future viewing. It does not reveal how preference was computed or how many ground-truth IDs the scorer retains. Our proposed “any ≥120-second qualifying airing” relevance set is therefore a transparent offline proxy, not a verified recreation of private labels. Do not claim public/private MAP equivalence based on the metric formula alone.

 ## 10. Recommended algorithms
+
+Implement the four planned methods in this order. The two qualifying exam methods are **program co-view PPR and Association Rules**. No method has been evaluated, and no performance claim is made.
+
+| Priority | Method | Proposed definition | Feasibility and limitations |
+|---|---|---|---|
+| 1 | Required popularity baseline | Distinct training users with qualifying program viewing; common tie/fallback rule | One pass over deduplicated user-item presence. Essential reference; not one of the two approved methods. |
+| 2 | Personal viewing frequency | Per-user count of distinct qualifying broadcasts of each ID, then shared fallback | Sparse lookup and ranking. Do not count raw fragments or conflate it with approved CF/MF. |
+| 3 | Personalized PageRank | Nodes are program IDs; weighted **program–program co-view** edges built from training users; restart distribution from that user's qualifying history | Meets the specified graph requirement. Avoid replacing it with user-user PageRank or a popularity-only random walk. |
+| 4 | Association Rules | Training user baskets, singleton antecedent/consequent rules `i→j` with support, confidence, lift | Approved method. Length-two itemsets keep computation bounded; this is a documented restricted rule-mining design, not a claim of full Apriori/FP-Growth enumeration. |
+
+### PPR specification to implement, not an executed experiment
+
+- Binary training incidence `X[u,i]`; integer co-view counts from `X.T @ X`, diagonal removed. Use at least int32 for counts, not uint8 multiplication that can overflow.
+- Initial edge weight proposal: cosine-normalized co-user support `co_count(i,j)/sqrt(support(i)*support(j))`; require at least three co-view users; retain top 100 neighbors per item, symmetrize explicitly, then row-normalize. Deterministic tie handling.
+- Personalized restart `s_u(i) ∝ log1p(qualifying_airing_count[u,i])` over training history. Initial damping α=0.85; dangling mass returns to `s_u`; iterate `p_next = α P.T p + (1−α)s_u` with the corresponding dangling correction.
+- Initial convergence settings: L1 tolerance `1e-8`, maximum 200 iterations, record convergence and wall time. Candidate restriction applies at ranking time, not by deleting all historical seed nodes from the graph. If seeds lack graph edges, use the documented dangling/fallback policy.
+- Small planned sensitivity grid: α in `{0.70,0.85}`, neighbor cap in `{50,100}` with other preprocessing fixed. All are untested configuration proposals.
+
+### Association-rule specification to implement
+
+- A basket is a user's distinct qualifying programs in the training window; each user contributes once to a pair's support. Define `N` as the 4,837 nonempty training baskets under the proposed threshold, recomputed by the production pipeline.
+- For pair count `n_ij`, `support=n_ij/N`, `confidence(i→j)=n_ij/n_i`, `lift=confidence/(n_j/N)`.
+- Initial rule filters: pair count ≥3, confidence ≥0.05, lift ≥1. Score a candidate by the sum over watched antecedents of normalized user-history weight × confidence × `log1p(lift)`; retain explanatory antecedents. A simple confidence-only alternative may be a separately logged ablation.
+- Candidate repeats remain permitted. Missing rules or fewer than five supported consequents use the exact shared fallback, not a special model-only policy. A small support-count grid `{3,5,10}` is sufficient initially; avoid exhaustive hyperparameter search before correctness checks.
+
+### Scale, memory, runtime
+
+The DST-aware 120-second audit found **716,796 training user-program pairs**, 4,837 nonempty users, and 2,948 watched items. Median user basket: 132 items; maximum: 1,171. Enumerating every user's unordered pair would emit **76,705,132 pair occurrences** before aggregation. A Python dictionary of every event/pair is unnecessary; sparse integer multiplication or streamed pair accumulation is preferable. Both PPR and rules may reuse training-only co-view statistics while retaining different, independently evaluated scoring mechanisms.
+
+Array-storage estimates, not measured model memory:
+- Training CSR with float32 values/int32 indices is roughly **5.49 MiB** excluding maps, intermediates, and overhead.
+- A dense 2,948² float32 item matrix is **33.15 MiB**; an 8,234² matrix is **258.63 MiB**. Dense co-occurrence intermediate storage is possible at this scale but sparse/pruned graphs give better headroom.
+- A directed top-100 graph over 8,234 items needs about 6.3 MiB for value/index arrays before symmetrization and overhead. Batch PPR by 32–64 users to bound workspace. A Python-object graph can consume much more memory than arrays.
+- Preprocessing diagnostics actually took minutes (§11). PPR cost is approximately `O(users × iterations × graph_edges)` without batching/reuse; rules' main cost is pair aggregation. Model wall times are **not measured yet**. Benchmark the initial configuration and cap grids before expanding scope.
+
+**Dependencies:** NumPy/SciPy for sparse arrays and numerical operations, pytest for meaningful verification; NetworkX could be a tiny-graph reference but is not installed and is not needed for the production graph. `mlxtend` is optional for a small rule-check reference, not necessary for pair rules. All are currently uninstalled in the inspected interpreter.
+
+**Defer until the mandatory comparison is verified:** CBF (sparse metadata and missing years), implicit MF/ALS (additional library/Python compatibility and hyperparameters), hybrids (evaluate individual components first; rank fusion avoids pretending raw scores are comparable). Do not create unused algorithm files now. The current diagnostic code uses only the standard library and no copied participant code.

The located homework rules explicitly identify invalid/fabricated/misattributed references (including broken URLs), claim–evidence mismatch, fabricated benchmarks, non-running solutions claimed to run, hallucinated APIs, materially wrong reasoning/root causes, claimed verification not performed, missing/noncorresponding session evidence, cherry-picked metrics, and a generic discussion without substantive 5-Loop engagement as major failures.

The audit is saved at:

**[`SWEETTV_Final_Exam/results/step1_audit.md`](SWEETTV_Final_Exam/results/step1_audit.md)**

It contains all 15 requested sections, detailed statistics, hashes, evaluation decisions, unresolved questions, and the Step 2 plan.

**No essential dataset is missing.**

### Can the data be processed?

**Yes.** Full streaming profiles and disk-backed duplicate/interval checks completed successfully. Peak memory for the most detailed inspection was approximately **515 MiB**.

Important findings:
- **17 duplicate viewing rows** and substantial overlapping viewing fragments require deduplication/interval union.
- **117 apparent duration discrepancies** are explained by the March 29 DST transition under a `Europe/Kyiv` interpretation. The timezone name remains an evidence-supported inference.
- Schedule files spill into adjacent weeks; validation must use **actual timestamps**, not filenames alone.
- Approximately **89% of schedule rows have ID `0`**, which must remain excluded from recommendable items.
- All template user IDs exceed floating-point exact-integer range and must be preserved as **strings**.
- A proposed **120-second per-user/per-airing threshold** retains 84.0% of positive training overlaps.

### Evaluation rules confirmed

The exam and presentation confirm:
- **MAP@5**, higher is better.
- AP normalization by **`min(5, number of relevant programs)`**.
- Exactly five ranked IDs, stored as **one space-separated field**.
- Common temporal evaluation and training-only model construction.

The timestamps support:
- Training: **March 9–May 17, 2020**
- Validation: **May 18–July 26, 2020**
- Final historical fitting: through **July 26**
- Test prediction: **July 27–October 18**

Kaggle’s detailed live scorer rules were **not independently retrievable**. Empty-label handling and hidden relevance construction are explicitly distinguished from the proposed local protocol.

### Implement first

1. **Popularity baseline** — mandatory.
2. **Personal viewing frequency** — additional reference.
3. **Program co-view Personalized PageRank** — approved method.
4. **Association Rules** — approved method.

Popularity and personal frequency do **not** satisfy the two-approved-method requirement.

### Risks to resolve

- Confirm live Kaggle evaluator details, account acceptance, and submission quota.
- Document the inferred timezone and test DST/boundary handling.
- Handle **10 training-cold template users** and **14 users without validation labels** consistently.
- Clarify the homework guidelines’ conflicting **five-page versus six-page** report limits.
- Complete genuine personal verification and preserve the final full-work session export.

### Integrity and session evidence

**All original files remained unchanged**, verified by closing SHA-256 comparisons. All **14 inspection-consistency checks passed**.

A native, unmodified OpenCode checkpoint was saved at:

`SWEETTV_Final_Exam/evidence/step1_opencode_session.json`

It is a checkpoint, not the eventual full-project export.

**Step 2 has not begun. No recommendation models were trained, no MAP results were claimed, and no Kaggle submission was generated.**

# SWEET.TV Final Exam — STEP 2

Continue the existing SWEET.TV OpenCode project.


Read the completed `results/step1_audit.md` and official `exam_quiz_FKN.md`.


Do not repeat Step 1 unnecessarily.


## Objective


Implement and independently verify the complete viewing-log-to-program interaction pipeline.


All Python implementation files must be created inside `code/`.


## Requirements


1. Preserve all five original Kaggle CSV files without modification.


2. Implement `code/data_pipeline.py` using the actual verified dataset schemas.


3. Preserve original user IDs exactly as strings.


4. Parse viewing timestamps and schedule timestamps explicitly.


5. Use the evidence-supported Europe/Kyiv-compatible timezone interpretation, clearly documented as an inference rather than an official rule.


6. Correctly handle daylight-saving transitions and broadcasts crossing temporal boundaries.


7. Match viewing intervals to program broadcasts using the same channel and positive interval overlap.


8. Remove exact duplicate viewing events and union overlapping viewing fragments to avoid double-counting seconds.


9. Aggregate viewing duration for each user and broadcast before applying the watched-program threshold.


10. Exclude `tv_show_id = 0` from recommendable items.


11. Implement the proposed 120-second threshold as a configurable parameter, not a hard-coded universal truth.


12. Preserve the ability to evaluate alternative thresholds without rebuilding the raw interval join.


13. Respect the chronological training, validation, and test boundaries from Step 1.


14. Never use future user viewing behavior when preparing training interactions.


15. Create reproducible derived-data outputs and statistics under `data/` and `results/`.


## Mandatory Verification


Implement independent tests covering:


- Correct channel matching.
- Exact interval-overlap calculation.
- Touching interval boundaries.
- Duplicate viewing records.
- Overlapping viewing fragments.
- Multiple viewing fragments of one broadcast.
- One viewing interval spanning multiple programs.
- Missing program IDs.
- Cold-start users.
- Daylight-saving transitions.
- Training and validation boundaries.
- Exact user ID preservation.


Compare the optimized matching implementation against a separate brute-force reference on small deterministic fixtures.


Record passed and failed checks.


## Deliverables


Create:


- `code/data_pipeline.py`
- Appropriate verification tests inside `tests/`
- Derived interaction files under `data/`
- `results/step2_preprocessing_report.md`
- `results/step2_verification.json`


The report must include real interaction counts, unique users, unique programs, missing-ID statistics, selected threshold, runtime, memory usage, failed tests, fixes, and reproducibility instructions.


Compare the measured data coverage with the Step 1 audit.


Investigate unexpected differences rather than silently accepting them.


## Important Restrictions


Do not implement PPR, Association Rules, Matrix Factorization, or hybrid models yet.


Do not calculate recommendation MAP@5 scores.


Do not generate a Kaggle submission.


Do not claim that local relevance labels reproduce hidden Kaggle labels unless verified.


Do not modify the original OpenCode session export.


## Final Response


Report:


1. Files created.
2. Interaction counts.
3. Training and validation coverage.
4. Missing-ID handling.
5. Viewing threshold.
6. Independent test results.
7. Runtime and memory usage.
8. Any unresolved problems.
9. Confirmation that original datasets remain unchanged.


Stop after Step 2.


Do not begin Step 3 automatically.

187: ## 4. Data-quality issues
188: 
189: 1. **DST rather than an unexplained duration error.** Naive subtraction disagrees with `duraton` in 117 rows, always by exactly +3,600 seconds. All 117 cross `2020-03-29 04:00:00`; no viewing start or stop occurs in local hour 03 that day. `Europe/Kyiv` localization followed by UTC subtraction matches every checked row near the transition (135,487 rows), and the full corrected diagnostic has zero duration mismatches. Across 394 schedule channel transitions, next-start minus current-start minus duration is also exactly 3,600 naive seconds. Example: channel 3, March 29 01:25, duration 6,000, next start 04:05. This strongly supports a skipped local hour, not arbitrary corrupted durations. The precise timezone name remains an inference, since several zones share this transition.
190: 2. **Do not add elapsed seconds on a naive/local wall clock across DST.** Localize schedule start, convert to UTC, then add duration on that UTC timeline; localize both viewing endpoints separately. Keep local calendar boundaries for the week split. Audit both parsed duration consistency and nonexistent/ambiguous times in Step 2.
191: 3. **17 exact duplicate viewing records.** Deduplicate derived data or union intervals; leave originals intact. The 17 rows do not explain all overlap inflation.
192: 4. **Substantial same-user/channel overlap and adjacency.** Unioning 5,821,987 raw intervals yields 5,441,773 segments (this reduction includes touching fragments). Same-channel duplicate/overlap time inflates naive summed elapsed viewing by **116,225,303 seconds**. Fragment counts must not be used as watch-frequency counts.
193: 5. **Concurrent different-channel viewing.** Summed per-user/channel union time is 8,502,989,921 seconds; union across all channels per user is 7,872,180,150 seconds. The 630,809,771-second excess demonstrates concurrency. The files do not identify devices or prove fraud. Keep channel-specific evidence for matching; do not invent a single-device sequence or sum this as unique human attention. Binary user support and qualifying-airing counts reduce duration inflation sensitivity.
194: 6. **Schedule gaps and missing channels.** Five viewed channels (`149, 1174, 1508, 1509, 1510`) are absent from both historical schedules, accounting for 113,579 view rows. Overall, 413,297 view rows have no schedule overlap under the DST-aware interpretation; some are gaps/coverage limitations on otherwise present channels. Do not label those rows as negative feedback or infer a program from a nearby title.
195: 7. **One zero-duration schedule row.** Early file, channel 644, `29.03.2020 04:00:00`, ID 0. Quarantine/drop from derived interval calculations. No negative IDs or other nonpositive intervals were observed; all view intervals are positive.
196: 8. **Schedule overlaps.** The naive per-file check found 2 / 2 / 8 rows overlapping earlier same-channel coverage, with 0 / 0 / 4 labelled-versus-labelled overlaps. Exact duplicate rows within each schedule are zero. Boundary raw-row comparisons across successive files found zero exact duplicates; on historically viewed channels, combined/deduplicated labelled airings had no overlaps under either tested clock interpretation. Still assert this property in the production join; do not silently double-credit conflicting program assignments if encountered. Future-schedule overlaps cannot supply future user labels.
197: 9. **IDs identify recurring programs, not necessarily a unique episode/title string.** Positive IDs with multiple titles: 1,685 / 2,508 / 1,679 per schedule file. Positive IDs with multiple categories within a file: zero. Use IDs as items; choose a documented representative historical title for display. Do not create new items solely from episode title variations.
198: 10. **Nine categories overall, eight among positive IDs.** All categories include `Музыка`; it does not occur among positive-ID rows in these files. Metadata is sparse and some years are ranges. CBF feasibility does not imply useful metadata for every item.
199: 11. **Selection and drift.** All recorded view durations exceed 60 seconds; this is an observed truncation, not a verified competition watched threshold. Weekly volume changes sharply: 105,223 starts in Week 27 versus 271,172 in Week 28. No causal explanation is established. The validation interval has fewer rows and longer overlap durations than training, so use a chronological evaluation and report limitations.

224: ## 6. Viewing-to-program matching design
225: 
226: ### Exact rule and double-count prevention
227: 
228: For view interval `V=[v_start,v_stop)` and airing `A=[a_start,a_start+duration)` on the same channel:
229: 
230: ```text
231: vsetv_id == channel_id
232: overlap_seconds = max(0, min(v_stop, a_end) - max(v_start, a_start))
233: ```
234: 
235: Use half-open intervals: touching endpoints have zero overlap. All interval arithmetic should use UTC elapsed seconds under the documented local-clock interpretation. Merely joining on channel/date or choosing the first broadcast after a view starts is incorrect.
236: 
237: Proposed processing order:
238: 
239: 1. Read exact string user IDs; parse both timestamp formats explicitly; check/record the timezone assumption. Reject/quarantine invalid spans without editing originals.
240: 2. Establish training/validation boundaries before any behavior aggregation. Clip viewing time to its period. The 1,007 raw intervals crossing the training cutoff contribute only their pre-cutoff portion to training; remaining time is validation evidence only.
241: 3. Deduplicate schedule airing identity `(channel_id, start_utc, end_utc, tv_show_id)` after comparing metadata; preserve conflict diagnostics. Boundary spillovers from the adjacent historical file can complete availability, but not expand behavior cutoffs.
242: 4. Group view fragments by `(user_id, channel_id)` within the period, union overlapping/touching fragments, then intersect with all eligible labelled airings. This avoids duplicate-time credit while allowing one long session to match multiple programs.
243: 5. Accumulate disjoint overlap pieces for each `(user_id, channel, airing_start, airing_end, tv_show_id, period)` before applying the watched threshold. Two short fragments of the same airing can jointly qualify. Do not add separate repeat broadcasts merely to pass a per-airing threshold.
244: 6. Count qualifying distinct airings for frequency, retain union seconds as an optional weight, and deduplicate `(user_id, program_id)` for binary relevance/support. Check total credited time per user-airing does not exceed its broadcast duration. If overlapping different labelled IDs exist on one channel, quarantine ambiguous time or resolve it explicitly and identically for all methods; historical diagnostics did not encounter this on viewed channels.
245: 
246: Avoid a Cartesian DataFrame join. Channel-sorted interval sweeps or start-time/prefix-max-end indexes plus bounded search are feasible. The inspection used SQLite ordering and per-channel interval indexes, not an exported interaction training set.

274: ## 7. MAP@5 definition
275: 
276: **Confirmed from the exam:** metric is MAP@K, higher is better, and this exam fixes K=5. **Confirmed from presentation pp.4–5:** normalize each user's AP by `min(K, |R_u|)`, then macro-average across users. The slides explicitly say to match the evaluator convention. The detailed live Kaggle scorer implementation was not retrievable, so empty-label/duplicate-prediction behavior and hidden relevance construction remain unconfirmed by the platform.
277: 
278: For the proposed local protocol, let `R_u` be the set of distinct positive program IDs with a qualifying validation airing, and `p_u[1:5]` the ordered predictions. Define `hit_u(r)=1` only for a relevant ID's first appearance; otherwise 0. Then:
279: 
280: ```text
281: P_u@r  = (sum_{j=1..r} hit_u(j)) / r
282: AP_u@5 = (sum_{r=1..5} P_u@r * hit_u(r)) / min(5, |R_u|), when |R_u| > 0
283: MAP@5  = (1 / |U|) * sum_{u in U} AP_u@5
284: ```
285: 
286: **Proposed edge policies:** empty `R_u` gives AP=0 for the primary all-user metric; duplicate predicted IDs cannot earn repeated hits and are rejected by the output validator; exactly five unique positive eligible IDs are required. Macro-average users, not views, and do not divide by the number of retrieved hits or by five when fewer than five relevant items exist.
287: 
288: The presentation's example is a useful future unit-test target: relevant `{A,B,C}`, ranking `A,B,D,C,E` gives `(1+1+3/4)/3 = 11/12`; `D,A,E,B,C` gives `(1/2+2/4+3/5)/3 = 8/15`. These are illustrative arithmetic examples, **not project experiment results or student personal verification**.
289: 
290: The slide's competition screenshot describes “five most preferred” programs from future viewing. It does not reveal how preference was computed or how many ground-truth IDs the scorer retains. Our proposed “any ≥120-second qualifying airing” relevance set is therefore a transparent offline proxy, not a verified recreation of private labels. Do not claim public/private MAP equivalence based on the metric formula alone.

307: ### Shared comparison contract (proposal)
308: 
309: - **Fit population:** all users with permitted training history, not just the test-template users. No validation history may create popularity counts, co-view edges, rules, user profiles, recency features, or hyperparameter-specific fitted statistics.
310: - **Primary evaluation users:** exactly the **1,260 original template users**, preserved as strings and in original order. This mirrors the known target cohort and keeps users fixed independently of model capability. Do not drop cold users to improve a score.
311: - **Relevance:** distinct positive IDs from ≥120 seconds of unioned overlap with at least one validation airing. No artificial truncation to five relevant items without confirmation of the hidden label rule.
312: - **Primary MAP:** all 1,260 users, empty relevance → AP=0. There are **1,246 nonempty-label users** and **14 empty-label users**. Report the count and also a clearly labelled nonempty-only MAP diagnostic for those same 1,246 users. The all-user theoretical ceiling from empty rows alone is 1,246/1,260 = 0.988889, not an achieved score.
313: - **Train history coverage:** 4,876 users have any training viewing; 4,837 have a ≥120-second labelled airing. Among template users, 1,256 have any training viewing and 1,250 have qualifying history: **10 cold users**, comprising four with no training viewing and six with viewing but no usable labelled overlap. Eight of the ten have nonempty validation relevance.
314: - **Final cold cases:** two template users have no ≥120-second labelled airing in either historical partition. Their histories require the shared fallback. This is a coverage diagnostic, not a final-model fitting result.
315: - **Common candidates, repeats, tie-breaking, fallback:** as in §9 for every method.
316: - **Selection:** a small predeclared hyperparameter grid, one common hold-out, all attempted comparisons retained. Select with MAP@5 and documented compute/coverage tradeoffs. Validation guides selection, never the fitted model's user-item statistics. Multiple trials on one hold-out are subject to selection optimism; disclose that limitation.
317: - **Final refit:** rebuild interactions over the entire history window, including recombining any airing fragments split by the now-removed validation boundary. Do not blindly concatenate thresholded train/validation tables, which could miss a boundary airing qualifying only in combination.
318: - Choose the same heavy and light/cold users from training-only history descriptors, with a deterministic rule and justification before looking for flattering recommendation examples. Compare their eventual lists against validation behavior, not inaccessible test outcomes.

332: **Allow previously watched programs for every method.** The exam does not forbid them. Among template users' 198,517 distinct validation user-program pairs at 120 seconds, 42,934 (21.63%) also occur in the same user's training history. This supports treating repeat consumption as possible; it is not a measured recommendation gain. “Allow repeats” means across time, not duplicate IDs inside one Top-5.
333: 
334: **Common fallback order, determined from training only:** candidate programs by descending distinct training-user support, then descending qualifying-airing count, then ascending numeric program ID. Cold items receive zero learned support and appear only after supported items unless a later individually evaluated method can score them. If all candidate supports are zero, deterministic ID ordering still provides five eligible IDs; no unrecorded random or future-popularity fallback is allowed.

336: **For every method:** filter IDs to the shared candidate catalog; remove 0 and duplicates; rank by method score with the same fallback ordering for ties; keep up to five positively supported method recommendations; fill missing slots from the common fallback without duplication. If a user lacks usable seeds/rules/graph reachability, return that fallback. Assert that at least five candidates exist; observed catalogs comfortably satisfy this. Do not treat independently scaled model scores as probabilities.

340: ## 10. Recommended algorithms
341: 
342: Implement the four planned methods in this order. The two qualifying exam methods are **program co-view PPR and Association Rules**. No method has been evaluated, and no performance claim is made.
343: 
344: | Priority | Method | Proposed definition | Feasibility and limitations |
345: |---|---|---|---|
346: | 1 | Required popularity baseline | Distinct training users with qualifying program viewing; common tie/fallback rule | One pass over deduplicated user-item presence. Essential reference; not one of the two approved methods. |
347: | 2 | Personal viewing frequency | Per-user count of distinct qualifying broadcasts of each ID, then shared fallback | Sparse lookup and ranking. Do not count raw fragments or conflate it with approved CF/MF. |
348: | 3 | Personalized PageRank | Nodes are program IDs; weighted **program–program co-view** edges built from training users; restart distribution from that user's qualifying history | Meets the specified graph requirement. Avoid replacing it with user-user PageRank or a popularity-only random walk. |
349: | 4 | Association Rules | Training user baskets, singleton antecedent/consequent rules `i→j` with support, confidence, lift | Approved method. Length-two itemsets keep computation bounded; this is a documented restricted rule-mining design, not a claim of full Apriori/FP-Growth enumeration. |

351: ### PPR specification to implement, not an executed experiment
352: 
353: - Binary training incidence `X[u,i]`; integer co-view counts from `X.T @ X`, diagonal removed. Use at least int32 for counts, not uint8 multiplication that can overflow.
354: - Initial edge weight proposal: cosine-normalized co-user support `co_count(i,j)/sqrt(support(i)*support(j))`; require at least three co-view users; retain top 100 neighbors per item, symmetrize explicitly, then row-normalize. Deterministic tie handling.
355: - Personalized restart `s_u(i) ∝ log1p(qualifying_airing_count[u,i])` over training history. Initial damping α=0.85; dangling mass returns to `s_u`; iterate `p_next = α P.T p + (1−α)s_u` with the corresponding dangling correction.
356: - Initial convergence settings: L1 tolerance `1e-8`, maximum 200 iterations, record convergence and wall time. Candidate restriction applies at ranking time, not by deleting all historical seed nodes from the graph. If seeds lack graph edges, use the documented dangling/fallback policy.
357: - Small planned sensitivity grid: α in `{0.70,0.85}`, neighbor cap in `{50,100}` with other preprocessing fixed. All are untested configuration proposals.

359: ### Association-rule specification to implement
360: 
361: - A basket is a user's distinct qualifying programs in the training window; each user contributes once to a pair's support. Define `N` as the 4,837 nonempty training baskets under the proposed threshold, recomputed by the production pipeline.
362: - For pair count `n_ij`, `support=n_ij/N`, `confidence(i→j)=n_ij/n_i`, `lift=confidence/(n_j/N)`.
363: - Initial rule filters: pair count ≥3, confidence ≥0.05, lift ≥1. Score a candidate by the sum over watched antecedents of normalized user-history weight × confidence × `log1p(lift)`; retain explanatory antecedents. A simple confidence-only alternative may be a separately logged ablation.
364: - Candidate repeats remain permitted. Missing rules or fewer than five supported consequents use the exact shared fallback, not a special model-only policy. A small support-count grid `{3,5,10}` is sufficient initially; avoid exhaustive hyperparameter search before correctness checks.
365: 
366: ### Scale, memory, runtime
367: 
368: The DST-aware 120-second audit found **716,796 training user-program pairs**, 4,837 nonempty users, and 2,948 watched items. Median user basket: 132 items; maximum: 1,171. Enumerating every user's unordered pair would emit **76,705,132 pair occurrences** before aggregation. A Python dictionary of every event/pair is unnecessary; sparse integer multiplication or streamed pair accumulation is preferable. Both PPR and rules may reuse training-only co-view statistics while retaining different, independently evaluated scoring mechanisms.
369: 
370: Array-storage estimates, not measured model memory:
371: - Training CSR with float32 values/int32 indices is roughly **5.49 MiB** excluding maps, intermediates, and overhead.
372: - A dense 2,948² float32 item matrix is **33.15 MiB**; an 8,234² matrix is **258.63 MiB**. Dense co-occurrence intermediate storage is possible at this scale but sparse/pruned graphs give better headroom.
373: - A directed top-100 graph over 8,234 items needs about 6.3 MiB for value/index arrays before symmetrization and overhead. Batch PPR by 32–64 users to bound workspace. A Python-object graph can consume much more memory than arrays.
374: - Preprocessing diagnostics actually took minutes (§11). PPR cost is approximately `O(users × iterations × graph_edges)` without batching/reuse; rules' main cost is pair aggregation. Model wall times are **not measured yet**. Benchmark the initial configuration and cap grids before expanding scope.

## 4. Data-quality issues

1. **DST rather than an unexplained duration error.** Naive subtraction disagrees with `duraton` in 117 rows, always by exactly +3,600 seconds. All 117 cross `2020-03-29 04:00:00`; no viewing start or stop occurs in local hour 03 that day. `Europe/Kyiv` localization followed by UTC subtraction matches every checked row near the transition (135,487 rows), and the full corrected diagnostic has zero duration mismatches. Across 394 schedule channel transitions, next-start minus current-start minus duration is also exactly 3,600 naive seconds. Example: channel 3, March 29 01:25, duration 6,000, next start 04:05. This strongly supports a skipped local hour, not arbitrary corrupted durations. The precise timezone name remains an inference, since several zones share this transition.
2. **Do not add elapsed seconds on a naive/local wall clock across DST.** Localize schedule start, convert to UTC, then add duration on that UTC timeline; localize both viewing endpoints separately. Keep local calendar boundaries for the week split. Audit both parsed duration consistency and nonexistent/ambiguous times in Step 2.
3. **17 exact duplicate viewing records.** Deduplicate derived data or union intervals; leave originals intact. The 17 rows do not explain all overlap inflation.
4. **Substantial same-user/channel overlap and adjacency.** Unioning 5,821,987 raw intervals yields 5,441,773 segments (this reduction includes touching fragments). Same-channel duplicate/overlap time inflates naive summed elapsed viewing by **116,225,303 seconds**. Fragment counts must not be used as watch-frequency counts.
5. **Concurrent different-channel viewing.** Summed per-user/channel union time is 8,502,989,921 seconds; union across all channels per user is 7,872,180,150 seconds. The 630,809,771-second excess demonstrates concurrency. The files do not identify devices or prove fraud. Keep channel-specific evidence for matching; do not invent a single-device sequence or sum this as unique human attention. Binary user support and qualifying-airing counts reduce duration inflation sensitivity.
6. **Schedule gaps and missing channels.** Five viewed channels (`149, 1174, 1508, 1509, 1510`) are absent from both historical schedules, accounting for 113,579 view rows. Overall, 413,297 view rows have no schedule overlap under the DST-aware interpretation; some are gaps/coverage limitations on otherwise present channels. Do not label those rows as negative feedback or infer a program from a nearby title.
7. **One zero-duration schedule row.** Early file, channel 644, `29.03.2020 04:00:00`, ID 0. Quarantine/drop from derived interval calculations. No negative IDs or other nonpositive intervals were observed; all view intervals are positive.
8. **Schedule overlaps.** The naive per-file check found 2 / 2 / 8 rows overlapping earlier same-channel coverage, with 0 / 0 / 4 labelled-versus-labelled overlaps. Exact duplicate rows within each schedule are zero. Boundary raw-row comparisons across successive files found zero exact duplicates; on historically viewed channels, combined/deduplicated labelled airings had no overlaps under either tested clock interpretation. Still assert this property in the production join; do not silently double-credit conflicting program assignments if encountered. Future-schedule overlaps cannot supply future user labels.
9. **IDs identify recurring programs, not necessarily a unique episode/title string.** Positive IDs with multiple titles: 1,685 / 2,508 / 1,679 per schedule file. Positive IDs with multiple categories within a file: zero. Use IDs as items; choose a documented representative historical title for display. Do not create new items solely from episode title variations.
10. **Nine categories overall, eight among positive IDs.** All categories include `Музыка`; it does not occur among positive-ID rows in these files. Metadata is sparse and some years are ranges. CBF feasibility does not imply useful metadata for every item.
11. **Selection and drift.** All recorded view durations exceed 60 seconds; this is an observed truncation, not a verified competition watched threshold. Weekly volume changes sharply: 105,223 starts in Week 27 versus 271,172 in Week 28. No causal explanation is established. The validation interval has fewer rows and longer overlap durations than training, so use a chronological evaluation and report limitations.

## 6. Viewing-to-program matching design

### Exact rule and double-count prevention

For view interval `V=[v_start,v_stop)` and airing `A=[a_start,a_start+duration)` on the same channel:

```text
vsetv_id == channel_id
overlap_seconds = max(0, min(v_stop, a_end) - max(v_start, a_start))
```

Use half-open intervals: touching endpoints have zero overlap. All interval arithmetic should use UTC elapsed seconds under the documented local-clock interpretation. Merely joining on channel/date or choosing the first broadcast after a view starts is incorrect.

Proposed processing order:

1. Read exact string user IDs; parse both timestamp formats explicitly; check/record the timezone assumption. Reject/quarantine invalid spans without editing originals.
2. Establish training/validation boundaries before any behavior aggregation. Clip viewing time to its period. The 1,007 raw intervals crossing the training cutoff contribute only their pre-cutoff portion to training; remaining time is validation evidence only.
3. Deduplicate schedule airing identity `(channel_id, start_utc, end_utc, tv_show_id)` after comparing metadata; preserve conflict diagnostics. Boundary spillovers from the adjacent historical file can complete availability, but not expand behavior cutoffs.
4. Group view fragments by `(user_id, channel_id)` within the period, union overlapping/touching fragments, then intersect with all eligible labelled airings. This avoids duplicate-time credit while allowing one long session to match multiple programs.
5. Accumulate disjoint overlap pieces for each `(user_id, channel, airing_start, airing_end, tv_show_id, period)` before applying the watched threshold. Two short fragments of the same airing can jointly qualify. Do not add separate repeat broadcasts merely to pass a per-airing threshold.
6. Count qualifying distinct airings for frequency, retain union seconds as an optional weight, and deduplicate `(user_id, program_id)` for binary relevance/support. Check total credited time per user-airing does not exceed its broadcast duration. If overlapping different labelled IDs exist on one channel, quarantine ambiguous time or resolve it explicitly and identically for all methods; historical diagnostics did not encounter this on viewed channels.

Avoid a Cartesian DataFrame join. Channel-sorted interval sweeps or start-time/prefix-max-end indexes plus bounded search are feasible. The inspection used SQLite ordering and per-channel interval indexes, not an exported interaction training set.

## 7. MAP@5 definition

**Confirmed from the exam:** metric is MAP@K, higher is better, and this exam fixes K=5. **Confirmed from presentation pp.4–5:** normalize each user's AP by `min(K, |R_u|)`, then macro-average across users. The slides explicitly say to match the evaluator convention. The detailed live Kaggle scorer implementation was not retrievable, so empty-label/duplicate-prediction behavior and hidden relevance construction remain unconfirmed by the platform.

For the proposed local protocol, let `R_u` be the set of distinct positive program IDs with a qualifying validation airing, and `p_u[1:5]` the ordered predictions. Define `hit_u(r)=1` only for a relevant ID's first appearance; otherwise 0. Then:

```text
P_u@r  = (sum_{j=1..r} hit_u(j)) / r
AP_u@5 = (sum_{r=1..5} P_u@r * hit_u(r)) / min(5, |R_u|), when |R_u| > 0
MAP@5  = (1 / |U|) * sum_{u in U} AP_u@5
```

**Proposed edge policies:** empty `R_u` gives AP=0 for the primary all-user metric; duplicate predicted IDs cannot earn repeated hits and are rejected by the output validator; exactly five unique positive eligible IDs are required. Macro-average users, not views, and do not divide by the number of retrieved hits or by five when fewer than five relevant items exist.

The presentation's example is a useful future unit-test target: relevant `{A,B,C}`, ranking `A,B,D,C,E` gives `(1+1+3/4)/3 = 11/12`; `D,A,E,B,C` gives `(1/2+2/4+3/5)/3 = 8/15`. These are illustrative arithmetic examples, **not project experiment results or student personal verification**.

The slide's competition screenshot describes “five most preferred” programs from future viewing. It does not reveal how preference was computed or how many ground-truth IDs the scorer retains. Our proposed “any ≥120-second qualifying airing” relevance set is therefore a transparent offline proxy, not a verified recreation of private labels. Do not claim public/private MAP equivalence based on the metric formula alone.

## 10. Recommended algorithms

Implement the four planned methods in this order. The two qualifying exam methods are **program co-view PPR and Association Rules**. No method has been evaluated, and no performance claim is made.

| Priority | Method | Proposed definition | Feasibility and limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Required popularity baseline | Distinct training users with qualifying program viewing; common tie/fallback rule | One pass over deduplicated user-item presence. Essential reference; not one of the two approved methods. |
| 2 | Personal viewing frequency | Per-user count of distinct qualifying broadcasts of each ID, then shared fallback | Sparse lookup and ranking. Do not count raw fragments or conflate it with approved CF/MF. |
| 3 | Personalized PageRank | Nodes are program IDs; weighted **program–program co-view** edges built from training users; restart distribution from that user's qualifying history | Meets the specified graph requirement. Avoid replacing it with user-user PageRank or a popularity-only random walk. |
| 4 | Association Rules | Training user baskets, singleton antecedent/consequent rules `i→j` with support, confidence, lift | Approved method. Length-two itemsets keep computation bounded; this is a documented restricted rule-mining design, not a claim of full Apriori/FP-Growth enumeration. |

### PPR specification to implement, not an executed experiment

- Binary training incidence `X[u,i]`; integer co-view counts from `X.T @ X`, diagonal removed. Use at least int32 for counts, not uint8 multiplication that can overflow.
- Initial edge weight proposal: cosine-normalized co-user support `co_count(i,j)/sqrt(support(i)*support(j))`; require at least three co-view users; retain top 100 neighbors per item, symmetrize explicitly, then row-normalize. Deterministic tie handling.
- Personalized restart `s_u(i) ∝ log1p(qualifying_airing_count[u,i])` over training history. Initial damping α=0.85; dangling mass returns to `s_u`; iterate `p_next = α P.T p + (1−α)s_u` with the corresponding dangling correction.
- Initial convergence settings: L1 tolerance `1e-8`, maximum 200 iterations, record convergence and wall time. Candidate restriction applies at ranking time, not by deleting all historical seed nodes from the graph. If seeds lack graph edges, use the documented dangling/fallback policy.
- Small planned sensitivity grid: α in `{0.70,0.85}`, neighbor cap in `{50,100}` with other preprocessing fixed. All are untested configuration proposals.

### Association-rule specification to implement

- A basket is a user's distinct qualifying programs in the training window; each user contributes once to a pair's support. Define `N` as the 4,837 nonempty training baskets under the proposed threshold, recomputed by the production pipeline.
- For pair count `n_ij`, `support=n_ij/N`, `confidence(i→j)=n_ij/n_i`, `lift=confidence/(n_j/N)`.
- Initial rule filters: pair count ≥3, confidence ≥0.05, lift ≥1. Score a candidate by the sum over watched antecedents of normalized user-history weight × confidence × `log1p(lift)`; retain explanatory antecedents. A simple confidence-only alternative may be a separately logged ablation.
- Candidate repeats remain permitted. Missing rules or fewer than five supported consequents use the exact shared fallback, not a special model-only policy. A small support-count grid `{3,5,10}` is sufficient initially; avoid exhaustive hyperparameter search before correctness checks.

### Scale, memory, runtime

The DST-aware 120-second audit found **716,796 training user-program pairs**, 4,837 nonempty users, and 2,948 watched items. Median user basket: 132 items; maximum: 1,171. Enumerating every user's unordered pair would emit **76,705,132 pair occurrences** before aggregation. A Python dictionary of every event/pair is unnecessary; sparse integer multiplication or streamed pair accumulation is preferable. Both PPR and rules may reuse training-only co-view statistics while retaining different, independently evaluated scoring mechanisms.

Array-storage estimates, not measured model memory:
- Training CSR with float32 values/int32 indices is roughly **5.49 MiB** excluding maps, intermediates, and overhead.
- A dense 2,948² float32 item matrix is **33.15 MiB**; an 8,234² matrix is **258.63 MiB**. Dense co-occurrence intermediate storage is possible at this scale but sparse/pruned graphs give better headroom.
- A directed top-100 graph over 8,234 items needs about 6.3 MiB for value/index arrays before symmetrization and overhead. Batch PPR by 32–64 users to bound workspace. A Python-object graph can consume much more memory than arrays.
- Preprocessing diagnostics actually took minutes (§11). PPR cost is approximately `O(users × iterations × graph_edges)` without batching/reuse; rules' main cost is pair aggregation. Model wall times are **not measured yet**. Benchmark the initial configuration and cap grids before expanding scope.

**Dependencies:** NumPy/SciPy for sparse arrays and numerical operations, pytest for meaningful verification; NetworkX could be a tiny-graph reference but is not installed and is not needed for the production graph. `mlxtend` is optional for a small rule-check reference, not necessary for pair rules. All are currently uninstalled in the inspected interpreter.

**Defer until the mandatory comparison is verified:** CBF (sparse metadata and missing years), implicit MF/ALS (additional library/Python compatibility and hyperparameters), hybrids (evaluate individual components first; rank fusion avoids pretending raw scores are comparable). Do not create unused algorithm files now. The current diagnostic code uses only the standard library and no copied participant code.

1: # Final Exam Quiz (FKN): TV Program Recommendation on sweet.tv
2: 
3: **Deadline:** 1 November 2026, 19:00 MSK. **Individual submission.**
4: 
5: ## 1. Purpose
6: 
7: Apply recommendation methods to an unfamiliar dataset, compare candidate methods fairly on one documented hold-out, and justify a final strategy for the platform. You will implement at least two methods, submit a ranked five-programme list per test user to Kaggle, and argue for a strategy a real service could adopt.
8: 
9: ## 2. The competition
10: 
11: - **Competition page:** [the competition page on Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/sweettv-tv-program-recommender) — title **sweet.tv — TV program recommender**, slug `sweettv-tv-program-recommender`, id 24201, host `ogurbych`, a community prediction competition.
12: - **Accept the rules first.** On that page open the *Rules* tab and click *I Understand and Accept* with your own Kaggle account. Until you do, the data download and the submit button both return 403. Acceptance is per account: your instructor's acceptance does not apply to yours.
13: - Metric: **MAP@{K}, higher is better**.
14: - **K = 5.** The page states the metric only as MAP@{K}. The submission template carries five space-separated programme ids per row, so this quiz fixes K = 5 to match the file you must produce. Use K = 5 everywhere: submission, hold-out, reported numbers.
15: - **The competition accepts late submissions.** The competition closed on 2020-11-21, but late submissions are still accepted and scored. Verified 2026-10-21: the unmodified template was submitted (ref 57484768) and returned status COMPLETE with **public 0.00000** and **private 0.00000**.
16: - **The leaderboard is frozen**, so a submission cannot change any standing. What matters here is the **returned private score**: the cohort ranking in §10 uses it, never your leaderboard position.
17: 
18: ## 3. Data
19: 
20: | File | Size | Rows | Role |
21: | --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
22: | `dataset11-30.csv` | 396 MB | 5,821,987 | view log |
23: | `export_arh_11-20-final.csv` | 153 MB | 1,074,235 | broadcast schedule, training weeks |
24: | `export_arh_21-30-final.csv` | 154 MB | 1,074,394 | broadcast schedule, training weeks |
25: | `export_arh_31-42-final.csv` | 186 MB | 1,295,378 | broadcast schedule, **test** weeks |
26: | `submission.csv` | — | 1,260 rows x 5 ids | template to fill |
27: 
28: Archive 131 MB, 890 MB extracted, 5 files, 9,265,994 rows across the four data files.
29: 
30: **View log columns:** `user_id, vsetv_id, start_time, stop_time, duraton`. `duraton` (misspelled in the file) is in seconds and equals `stop_time` minus `start_time` — the length of the viewing interval, **not** the length of the programme. Median 396 s, max 342,145 s.
31: 
32: **Schedule columns:** `channel_id, channel_title, start_time, duration, tv_show_title, tv_show_id, tv_show_category, tv_show_genre_1, tv_show_genre_2, tv_show_genre_3, year_of_production, director, actors`.
33: 
34: **Scale and coverage:** 5,848 / 6,364 / 6,637 distinct programmes per schedule file; 400 / 403 / 404 channels; 9 categories.
35: 
36: **The labelling caveat that shapes this task: only 10.8% of schedule rows carry a programme id.** In weeks 11-20, 115,613 of 1,074,235 rows have `tv_show_id != 0`; the other 958,622 are unlabelled airtime (`tv_show_id = 0`). Most of the grid has a channel, a time slot and a title but **no programme id**, so only labelled rows can become an item.
37: 
38: **Reading cost:** all four files read with the standard-library `csv` module in about 4.6 s at 12.6 MB peak memory. Repeated passes are cheap, so prefer a streaming design and document your environment.
39: 
40: **Your task is a join, then a prediction.** Join the view log to the schedule — same channel, and the user's view interval overlapping a programme's airing interval — to obtain user-programme interactions. Then predict, for each of the 1,260 test users, the five programmes they will watch in weeks 31-42.
41: 
42: Two consequences to plan for. The test weeks are **later than all training weeks**, so every method must extrapolate forward. And any user absent from the training window, or whose history touches only unlabelled airtime, is a **cold-start** case with no usable interactions.
43: 
44: ## 4. Implementation task
45: 
46: Implement **at least two** of:
47: 
48: 1. **Content-based filtering.** Now allowed, because the schedule supplies `tv_show_category`, three genre fields, `year_of_production`, `director` and `actors`. Build item vectors from these attributes and a user profile from that user's watched items.
49: 2. **Association rules** over each user's history or time windows.
50: 3. **Matrix factorization** for implicit feedback over user-programme counts, plain or duration-weighted, since no rating scale exists.
51: 4. **Personalized PageRank** on a programme co-view graph, personalised from each user's history.
52: 
53: A popularity or mean baseline does **not** count as one of your two methods, but a **popularity baseline is required** as the reference every method is measured against.
54: 
55: ## 5. Common requirements
56: 
57: - **Define how a viewing is matched to a programme.** State the join rule (channel plus interval overlap) and the threshold you use to call an overlap "watched". The data has **no programme-length-normalised watch percentage built in**, so you must construct any normalisation yourself and justify it against the observed duration distribution — an absolute-seconds cut and a fraction-of-`duration` cut are both defensible, but you must say which you used and why.
58: - **State how `tv_show_id = 0` rows are handled.** They are unlabelled airtime, not items. Say whether you drop them, use them as watching context, or treat them as misses.
59: - **Define your own validation split and justify it.** The test window is weeks 31-42, so validation must come from weeks 21-30 or earlier. Preserve temporal order.
60: - **Build every model from training data only.** Validation is for selection, never fitting.
61: - **Define the candidate pool.** It is bounded by the labelled programmes in the schedule; state whether recommending an already-watched programme is allowed. The competition does not forbid repeats; your choice must be explicit and identical across methods.
62: - **Handle users with no history.** State exactly what your system returns for them, and why — and give the same fallback everywhere.
63: - **Explain how each method produces exactly five programme ids.** Scores from different methods are not interchangeable probabilities — say how each output becomes a ranked list of five.
64: - **Document** hyperparameters, random seeds, runtime and environment.
65: - **Never use future viewing behaviour.** A user's views in the test window (weeks 31-42) may not be used in training or in any feature. The test-period schedule may be used only to know which programme airs on which channel at which time; it must never be used to look up who watched what.
66: 
67: ## 6. Final strategy

# Final Exam Quiz (FKN): TV Program Recommendation on sweet.tv

**Deadline:** 1 November 2026, 19:00 MSK. **Individual submission.**

## 1. Purpose

Apply recommendation methods to an unfamiliar dataset, compare candidate methods fairly on one documented hold-out, and justify a final strategy for the platform. You will implement at least two methods, submit a ranked five-programme list per test user to Kaggle, and argue for a strategy a real service could adopt.

## 2. The competition

- **Competition page:** [the competition page on Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/sweettv-tv-program-recommender) — title **sweet.tv — TV program recommender**, slug `sweettv-tv-program-recommender`, id 24201, host `ogurbych`, a community prediction competition.
- **Accept the rules first.** On that page open the *Rules* tab and click *I Understand and Accept* with your own Kaggle account. Until you do, the data download and the submit button both return 403. Acceptance is per account: your instructor's acceptance does not apply to yours.
- Metric: **MAP@{K}, higher is better**.
- **K = 5.** The page states the metric only as MAP@{K}. The submission template carries five space-separated programme ids per row, so this quiz fixes K = 5 to match the file you must produce. Use K = 5 everywhere: submission, hold-out, reported numbers.
- **The competition accepts late submissions.** The competition closed on 2020-11-21, but late submissions are still accepted and scored. Verified 2026-10-21: the unmodified template was submitted (ref 57484768) and returned status COMPLETE with **public 0.00000** and **private 0.00000**.
- **The leaderboard is frozen**, so a submission cannot change any standing. What matters here is the **returned private score**: the cohort ranking in §10 uses it, never your leaderboard position.

## 3. Data

| File | Size | Rows | Role |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `dataset11-30.csv` | 396 MB | 5,821,987 | view log |
| `export_arh_11-20-final.csv` | 153 MB | 1,074,235 | broadcast schedule, training weeks |
| `export_arh_21-30-final.csv` | 154 MB | 1,074,394 | broadcast schedule, training weeks |
| `export_arh_31-42-final.csv` | 186 MB | 1,295,378 | broadcast schedule, **test** weeks |
| `submission.csv` | — | 1,260 rows x 5 ids | template to fill |

Archive 131 MB, 890 MB extracted, 5 files, 9,265,994 rows across the four data files.

**View log columns:** `user_id, vsetv_id, start_time, stop_time, duraton`. `duraton` (misspelled in the file) is in seconds and equals `stop_time` minus `start_time` — the length of the viewing interval, **not** the length of the programme. Median 396 s, max 342,145 s.

**Schedule columns:** `channel_id, channel_title, start_time, duration, tv_show_title, tv_show_id, tv_show_category, tv_show_genre_1, tv_show_genre_2, tv_show_genre_3, year_of_production, director, actors`.

**Scale and coverage:** 5,848 / 6,364 / 6,637 distinct programmes per schedule file; 400 / 403 / 404 channels; 9 categories.

**The labelling caveat that shapes this task: only 10.8% of schedule rows carry a programme id.** In weeks 11-20, 115,613 of 1,074,235 rows have `tv_show_id != 0`; the other 958,622 are unlabelled airtime (`tv_show_id = 0`). Most of the grid has a channel, a time slot and a title but **no programme id**, so only labelled rows can become an item.

**Reading cost:** all four files read with the standard-library `csv` module in about 4.6 s at 12.6 MB peak memory. Repeated passes are cheap, so prefer a streaming design and document your environment.

**Your task is a join, then a prediction.** Join the view log to the schedule — same channel, and the user's view interval overlapping a programme's airing interval — to obtain user-programme interactions. Then predict, for each of the 1,260 test users, the five programmes they will watch in weeks 31-42.

Two consequences to plan for. The test weeks are **later than all training weeks**, so every method must extrapolate forward. And any user absent from the training window, or whose history touches only unlabelled airtime, is a **cold-start** case with no usable interactions.

## 4. Implementation task

Implement **at least two** of:

1. **Content-based filtering.** Now allowed, because the schedule supplies `tv_show_category`, three genre fields, `year_of_production`, `director` and `actors`. Build item vectors from these attributes and a user profile from that user's watched items.
2. **Association rules** over each user's history or time windows.
3. **Matrix factorization** for implicit feedback over user-programme counts, plain or duration-weighted, since no rating scale exists.
4. **Personalized PageRank** on a programme co-view graph, personalised from each user's history.

A popularity or mean baseline does **not** count as one of your two methods, but a **popularity baseline is required** as the reference every method is measured against.

## 5. Common requirements

- **Define how a viewing is matched to a programme.** State the join rule (channel plus interval overlap) and the threshold you use to call an overlap "watched". The data has **no programme-length-normalised watch percentage built in**, so you must construct any normalisation yourself and justify it against the observed duration distribution — an absolute-seconds cut and a fraction-of-`duration` cut are both defensible, but you must say which you used and why.
- **State how `tv_show_id = 0` rows are handled.** They are unlabelled airtime, not items. Say whether you drop them, use them as watching context, or treat them as misses.
- **Define your own validation split and justify it.** The test window is weeks 31-42, so validation must come from weeks 21-30 or earlier. Preserve temporal order.
- **Build every model from training data only.** Validation is for selection, never fitting.
- **Define the candidate pool.** It is bounded by the labelled programmes in the schedule; state whether recommending an already-watched programme is allowed. The competition does not forbid repeats; your choice must be explicit and identical across methods.
- **Handle users with no history.** State exactly what your system returns for them, and why — and give the same fallback everywhere.
- **Explain how each method produces exactly five programme ids.** Scores from different methods are not interchangeable probabilities — say how each output becomes a ranked list of five.
- **Document** hyperparameters, random seeds, runtime and environment.
- **Never use future viewing behaviour.** A user's views in the test window (weeks 31-42) may not be used in training or in any feature. The test-period schedule may be used only to know which programme airs on which channel at which time; it must never be used to look up who watched what.

## 6. Final strategy

Submit one implemented method, or a hybrid combining methods by score fusion, rank fusion, candidate generation with re-ranking, or a documented switching rule. For a hybrid, state its components, how weights or thresholds were chosen, and how it compares with each individual method on the hold-out. A hybrid is optional; combining two methods without implementing and evaluating each one individually does not satisfy the comparison requirement.

## 7. Recommendation examples

Choose **two users yourself** and justify the choice — for example one heavy and one light viewer, or one user with no usable history. Use the **same two users across all methods**. For each user, show **each method's** Top-5 in order, with the programme id, the title and the category looked up from the schedule, so the methods can be read side by side. Reproduce the ids in your report. If a method cannot fill five slots, say so and explain the fallback.

## 8. Business and algorithmic analysis — one required question

**Which recommendation strategy would you select for this platform, and why?**

Using the same two users, compare each method's five ids against what those users actually watched, and discuss:

- whether the lists reflect familiar preferences or offer relevant new programmes;
- how and why the methods differ — what association rules capture that matrix factorization misses, what content attributes contribute where co-view signal is thin, how PageRank's graph diffusion reshapes the ranking, and where the popularity baseline already does well;
- why your final strategy is preferable, considering validation performance, computational cost at this scale, and what the lists imply for the user experience;
- limitations and failure cases your results actually support — beginning with the fact that only 10.8% of airtime carries an id.

Two cautions. An unfamiliar programme is **not** automatically a useful discovery — it may simply be a poor recommendation, and nothing here reveals whether a user enjoyed it. And absence from the log does not establish that a user has never seen a programme: the log records this platform's views only. Qualify "never", "always" and "better" to the evidence and scope you examined.

**No live A/B test, online experiment or revenue claim is required — and none may be claimed.** Every assertion must follow from the supplied data and your implementation.

## 9. Submission

Submit exactly two files:
- your report as a **PDF**;
- the **original, unmodified AI-session export**.

Nothing else is submitted through the course channel. The Kaggle submission file belongs in your repository, not in the submission.

**The PDF must contain:**
- a link to your **GitHub repository**;
- a **screenshot** showing the returned Kaggle private score of your designated final submission (a written score alone is not sufficient);
- your method comparison, validation results, and the business and algorithmic analysis.

**The GitHub repository must contain:** your implementation code; instructions for reproducing the results (optional); and the final submission file used to obtain the reported Kaggle score.

The homework format applies otherwise unchanged: course report, and the records the existing homework guidelines require. This quiz adds no new language requirement, page limit or replacement rubric. Disclose external code, models, data and assistance as the homework instructions and competition rules require. Do not fabricate experiments, references or results.

**Gate 0 is an automatic fail of the exam.** Re-read the homework guidelines before submitting. Fabricated experiments or references, a claim of verification you did not perform, and an AI-session export that does not correspond to the work all trigger it.

## 10. Grading — 100 points

### A. Kaggle private-score ranking within the exam cohort — 50 points

Students are ranked **within this exam cohort**, never against the original Kaggle participants, by the **returned private score** of their designated submission. The leaderboard is frozen, so position on it carries no information; only the returned score does. The metric is MAP@{K} with **higher is better**, so 0.00000 is the worst possible score rather than a neutral one — the template's own 0.00000 makes that concrete.

| Cohort band (by returned private score, best first) | Points |
| --- | ---: |
| Top 20% | 50 |

| Next 20% | 30 |
| Next 20% | 20 |
| Bottom 20% | 10 |

### B. Homework-style evaluation — 50 points

The existing homework criteria apply, scaled to 50 points, covering implementation, report, verification, business analysis and the required records. This quiz does not invent a new subscore breakdown. A high private score does not replace the requirement to implement and compare two methods, justify the strategy, and provide evidence.
