# Final Exam Quiz (FKN): TV Program Recommendation on sweet.tv

**Deadline:** 1 November 2026, 19:00 MSK. **Individual submission.**

## 1. Purpose

Apply recommendation methods to an unfamiliar dataset, compare candidate methods fairly on one documented hold-out, and justify a final strategy for the platform. You will implement at least two methods, submit a ranked five-programme list per test user to Kaggle, and argue for a strategy a real service could adopt.

## 2. The competition

- **Competition page:** [the competition page on Kaggle](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/sweettv-tv-program-recommender) — title **sweet.tv — TV program recommender**, slug `sweettv-tv-program-recommender`, id 24201, host `ogurbych`, a community prediction competition.
- **Accept the rules first.** On that page open the *Rules* tab and click *I Understand and Accept* with your own Kaggle account. Until you do, the data download and the submit button both return 403. Acceptance is per account: your instructor's acceptance does not apply to yours.
- Metric: **MAP@{K}, higher is better**.
- **K = 5.** The page states the metric only as MAP@{K}. The submission template carries five space-separated programme ids per row, so this quiz fixes K = 5 to match the file you must produce. Use K = 5 everywhere: submission, hold-out, reported numbers.
- **The competition accepts late submissions.** The competition closed on 2020-11-21, but late submissions are still accepted and scored. Verified 2026-10-21: the unmodified template was submitted (ref 57484768) and returned status COMPLETE with **public 0.00000** and **private 0.00000**.
- **The leaderboard is frozen**, so a submission cannot change any standing. What matters here is the **returned private score**: the cohort ranking in §10 uses it, never your leaderboard position.

## 3. Data

| File | Size | Rows | Role |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `dataset11-30.csv` | 396 MB | 5,821,987 | view log |
| `export_arh_11-20-final.csv` | 153 MB | 1,074,235 | broadcast schedule, training weeks |
| `export_arh_21-30-final.csv` | 154 MB | 1,074,394 | broadcast schedule, training weeks |
| `export_arh_31-42-final.csv` | 186 MB | 1,295,378 | broadcast schedule, **test** weeks |
| `submission.csv` | — | 1,260 rows x 5 ids | template to fill |

Archive 131 MB, 890 MB extracted, 5 files, 9,265,994 rows across the four data files.

**View log columns:** `user_id, vsetv_id, start_time, stop_time, duraton`. `duraton` (misspelled in the file) is in seconds and equals `stop_time` minus `start_time` — the length of the viewing interval, **not** the length of the programme. Median 396 s, max 342,145 s.

**Schedule columns:** `channel_id, channel_title, start_time, duration, tv_show_title, tv_show_id, tv_show_category, tv_show_genre_1, tv_show_genre_2, tv_show_genre_3, year_of_production, director, actors`.

**Scale and coverage:** 5,848 / 6,364 / 6,637 distinct programmes per schedule file; 400 / 403 / 404 channels; 9 categories.

**The labelling caveat that shapes this task: only 10.8% of schedule rows carry a programme id.** In weeks 11-20, 115,613 of 1,074,235 rows have `tv_show_id != 0`; the other 958,622 are unlabelled airtime (`tv_show_id = 0`). Most of the grid has a channel, a time slot and a title but **no programme id**, so only labelled rows can become an item.

**Reading cost:** all four files read with the standard-library `csv` module in about 4.6 s at 12.6 MB peak memory. Repeated passes are cheap, so prefer a streaming design and document your environment.

**Your task is a join, then a prediction.** Join the view log to the schedule — same channel, and the user's view interval overlapping a programme's airing interval — to obtain user-programme interactions. Then predict, for each of the 1,260 test users, the five programmes they will watch in weeks 31-42.

Two consequences to plan for. The test weeks are **later than all training weeks**, so every method must extrapolate forward. And any user absent from the training window, or whose history touches only unlabelled airtime, is a **cold-start** case with no usable interactions.

## 4. Implementation task

Implement **at least two** of:

1. **Content-based filtering.** Now allowed, because the schedule supplies `tv_show_category`, three genre fields, `year_of_production`, `director` and `actors`. Build item vectors from these attributes and a user profile from that user's watched items.
2. **Association rules** over each user's history or time windows.
3. **Matrix factorization** for implicit feedback over user-programme counts, plain or duration-weighted, since no rating scale exists.
4. **Personalized PageRank** on a programme co-view graph, personalised from each user's history.

A popularity or mean baseline does **not** count as one of your two methods, but a **popularity baseline is required** as the reference every method is measured against.

## 5. Common requirements

- **Define how a viewing is matched to a programme.** State the join rule (channel plus interval overlap) and the threshold you use to call an overlap "watched". The data has **no programme-length-normalised watch percentage built in**, so you must construct any normalisation yourself and justify it against the observed duration distribution — an absolute-seconds cut and a fraction-of-`duration` cut are both defensible, but you must say which you used and why.
- **State how `tv_show_id = 0` rows are handled.** They are unlabelled airtime, not items. Say whether you drop them, use them as watching context, or treat them as misses.
- **Define your own validation split and justify it.** The test window is weeks 31-42, so validation must come from weeks 21-30 or earlier. Preserve temporal order.
- **Build every model from training data only.** Validation is for selection, never fitting.
- **Define the candidate pool.** It is bounded by the labelled programmes in the schedule; state whether recommending an already-watched programme is allowed. The competition does not forbid repeats; your choice must be explicit and identical across methods.
- **Handle users with no history.** State exactly what your system returns for them, and why — and give the same fallback everywhere.
- **Explain how each method produces exactly five programme ids.** Scores from different methods are not interchangeable probabilities — say how each output becomes a ranked list of five.
- **Document** hyperparameters, random seeds, runtime and environment.
- **Never use future viewing behaviour.** A user's views in the test window (weeks 31-42) may not be used in training or in any feature. The test-period schedule may be used only to know which programme airs on which channel at which time; it must never be used to look up who watched what.

## 6. Final strategy

Submit one implemented method, or a hybrid combining methods by score fusion, rank fusion, candidate generation with re-ranking, or a documented switching rule. For a hybrid, state its components, how weights or thresholds were chosen, and how it compares with each individual method on the hold-out. A hybrid is optional; combining two methods without implementing and evaluating each one individually does not satisfy the comparison requirement.

## 7. Recommendation examples

Choose **two users yourself** and justify the choice — for example one heavy and one light viewer, or one user with no usable history. Use the **same two users across all methods**. For each user, show **each method's** Top-5 in order, with the programme id, the title and the category looked up from the schedule, so the methods can be read side by side. Reproduce the ids in your report. If a method cannot fill five slots, say so and explain the fallback.

## 8. Business and algorithmic analysis — one required question

**Which recommendation strategy would you select for this platform, and why?**

Using the same two users, compare each method's five ids against what those users actually watched, and discuss:

- whether the lists reflect familiar preferences or offer relevant new programmes;
- how and why the methods differ — what association rules capture that matrix factorization misses, what content attributes contribute where co-view signal is thin, how PageRank's graph diffusion reshapes the ranking, and where the popularity baseline already does well;
- why your final strategy is preferable, considering validation performance, computational cost at this scale, and what the lists imply for the user experience;
- limitations and failure cases your results actually support — beginning with the fact that only 10.8% of airtime carries an id.

Two cautions. An unfamiliar programme is **not** automatically a useful discovery — it may simply be a poor recommendation, and nothing here reveals whether a user enjoyed it. And absence from the log does not establish that a user has never seen a programme: the log records this platform's views only. Qualify "never", "always" and "better" to the evidence and scope you examined.

**No live A/B test, online experiment or revenue claim is required — and none may be claimed.** Every assertion must follow from the supplied data and your implementation.

## 9. Submission

Submit exactly two files:
- your report as a **PDF**;
- the **original, unmodified AI-session export**.

Nothing else is submitted through the course channel. The Kaggle submission file belongs in your repository, not in the submission.

**The PDF must contain:**
- a link to your **GitHub repository**;
- a **screenshot** showing the returned Kaggle private score of your designated final submission (a written score alone is not sufficient);
- your method comparison, validation results, and the business and algorithmic analysis.

**The GitHub repository must contain:** your implementation code; instructions for reproducing the results (optional); and the final submission file used to obtain the reported Kaggle score.

The homework format applies otherwise unchanged: course report, and the records the existing homework guidelines require. This quiz adds no new language requirement, page limit or replacement rubric. Disclose external code, models, data and assistance as the homework instructions and competition rules require. Do not fabricate experiments, references or results.

**Gate 0 is an automatic fail of the exam.** Re-read the homework guidelines before submitting. Fabricated experiments or references, a claim of verification you did not perform, and an AI-session export that does not correspond to the work all trigger it.

## 10. Grading — 100 points

### A. Kaggle private-score ranking within the exam cohort — 50 points

Students are ranked **within this exam cohort**, never against the original Kaggle participants, by the **returned private score** of their designated submission. The leaderboard is frozen, so position on it carries no information; only the returned score does. The metric is MAP@{K} with **higher is better**, so 0.00000 is the worst possible score rather than a neutral one — the template's own 0.00000 makes that concrete.

| Cohort band (by returned private score, best first) | Points |
| --- | ---: |
| Top 20% | 50 |
| Next 20% | 40 |
| Next 20% | 30 |
| Next 20% | 20 |
| Bottom 20% | 10 |

### B. Homework-style evaluation — 50 points

The existing homework criteria apply, scaled to 50 points, covering implementation, report, verification, business analysis and the required records. This quiz does not invent a new subscore breakdown. A high private score does not replace the requirement to implement and compare two methods, justify the strategy, and provide evidence.

225: 
226: ### Exact rule and double-count prevention
227: 
228: For view interval `V=[v_start,v_stop)` and airing `A=[a_start,a_start+duration)` on the same channel:
229: 
230: ```text
231: vsetv_id == channel_id
232: overlap_seconds = max(0, min(v_stop, a_end) - max(v_start, a_start))
233: ```
234: 
235: Use half-open intervals: touching endpoints have zero overlap. All interval arithmetic should use UTC elapsed seconds under the documented local-clock interpretation. Merely joining on channel/date or choosing the first broadcast after a view starts is incorrect.

238: 
239: 1. Read exact string user IDs; parse both timestamp formats explicitly; check/record the timezone assumption. Reject/quarantine invalid spans without editing originals.
240: 2. Establish training/validation boundaries before any behavior aggregation. Clip viewing time to its period. The 1,007 raw intervals crossing the training cutoff contribute only their pre-cutoff portion to training; remaining time is validation evidence only.
241: 3. Deduplicate schedule airing identity `(channel_id, start_utc, end_utc, tv_show_id)` after comparing metadata; preserve conflict diagnostics. Boundary spillovers from the adjacent historical file can complete availability, but not expand behavior cutoffs.
242: 4. Group view fragments by `(user_id, channel_id)` within the period, union overlapping/touching fragments, then intersect with all eligible labelled airings. This avoids duplicate-time credit while allowing one long session to match multiple programs.
243: 5. Accumulate disjoint overlap pieces for each `(user_id, channel, airing_start, airing_end, tv_show_id, period)` before applying the watched threshold. Two short fragments of the same airing can jointly qualify. Do not add separate repeat broadcasts merely to pass a per-airing threshold.

CSV has no embedded type schema. The following are inspected semantic types and proposed safe storage, not a claim that pandas inferred them:

**View log**, in original order:

| Column | Observed representation | Safe interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| `user_id` | Unsigned decimal integer text | Exact string key; never float or signed int64 |
| `vsetv_id` | Integer text | Channel integer, joins `channel_id` |
| `start_time` | `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS` | Explicitly parsed local timestamp; timezone inference discussed below |
| `stop_time` | Same format | Viewing stop timestamp |
| `duraton` | Integer text | Elapsed viewing seconds; preserve the original misspelling |

**All schedules**, identical order/schema:

`channel_id, channel_title, start_time, duration, tv_show_title, tv_show_id, tv_show_category, tv_show_genre_1, tv_show_genre_2, tv_show_genre_3, year_of_production, director, actors`.

- `channel_id`, `duration`, `tv_show_id`: integer-form values; safe integer conversion after validation. `duration` is broadcast elapsed seconds.
- `start_time`: `DD.MM.YYYY HH:MM:SS`; explicit day-first parse, not automatic month/day inference.
- All title/category/genre/director/actor fields: UTF-8 strings, nullable where indicated below. Quoted commas in titles/cast require a real CSV parser.
- `year_of_production`: nullable **text**, not an integer column. Nonnumeric nonempty rows: 53,616 / 51,935 / 64,162. Examples include `1996-`, `2012-2012`, `2014-`. Any later feature extraction must preserve raw text and document start/end-year parsing.

**Template:** `user_id` is exact decimal-string identity; `tv_show_id` is a **single string containing five space-separated integer tokens**, not five CSV columns. All 1,260 rows contain `0 0 0 0 0`. Header is exactly `user_id,tv_show_id`. No duplicate users, empty cells, or malformed token counts were found. Preserve original row order as well as original IDs in a later output; write no DataFrame index.

**ID precision:** view-user range is `2244466330591177`–`18443832178892490378`; 4,912 unique IDs exceed 2^53 and 2,483 exceed signed int64. Template range is `36938861791891792`–`18440717181607000261`; **all 1,260 exceed 2^53**, and **655 exceed signed int64**. String keys avoid rounding, overflow, and spreadsheet scientific-notation conversions. All template users occur somewhere in the view log. No leading-zero user IDs were observed, but strings also preserve them if future files contain any.

### Missing values

Empty/whitespace-only values were counted in every field. No whitespace-only nonempty cells or literal `null`, `none`, `nan`, `na`, `n/a` markers were found. Zero is **not** treated as an empty CSV cell.

- View log: **0 missing** in all five columns.
- Template: **0 missing** in both columns.
- Schedule columns `channel_id`, `channel_title`, `start_time`, `duration`, `tv_show_title`, `tv_show_id`, `tv_show_category`: **0 missing in each file**.

| Nullable schedule column | Weeks 11–20 file | Weeks 21–30 file | Weeks 31–42 file |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `tv_show_genre_1` | 620,089 | 616,370 | 737,871 |
| `tv_show_genre_2` | 928,009 | 924,020 | 1,113,598 |
| `tv_show_genre_3` | 1,054,059 | 1,050,668 | 1,266,621 |
| `year_of_production` | 959,500 | 954,382 | 1,151,706 |
| `director` | 974,050 | 969,487 | 1,170,189 |
| `actors` | 973,861 | 968,834 | 1,169,519 |

### Actual timestamp coverage (as written, local wall clock)

| File | Earliest start | Latest start | Latest end |
|---|---|---|---|
| Views | 2020-03-09 00:00:02 | 2020-07-26 23:58:42 | 2020-07-26 23:59:58 |
| Schedule 11–20 | 2020-03-08 23:00:00 | 2020-05-18 11:45:00 | 2020-05-18 12:00:00 |
| Schedule 21–30 | 2020-05-18 00:00:00 | 2020-07-27 11:55:00 | 2020-07-27 12:00:00 |
| Schedule 31–42 | 2020-07-27 00:00:00 | 2020-10-19 11:55:00 | 2020-10-19 12:00:00 |
| Template | N/A | N/A | N/A |

Schedule ends are inferred from start plus broadcast duration; extrema above are unchanged by the DST correction. The first profile's naive end calculations around March 29 are superseded by the timezone-aware diagnostic, not by modifying the raw CSV.

Viewing starts occupy ISO weeks 11–30 of **2020**, not 2026. The early schedule has 86 starts in Week 10 and 2,431 in Week 21; the next has 2,429 in Week 31; the future file has 2,399 in Week 43. Filenames are not sufficient filters.

### Duration distributions (seconds; exact nearest-rank quantiles)

| Input duration | Minimum | P25 | Median | P75 | P90 | P95 | P99 | Maximum |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Viewing `duraton` | 61 | 133 | 396 | 1,452 | 3,911 | 6,344 | 14,080 | 342,145 |
| Broadcast 11–20 | 0 | 600 | 1,500 | 3,000 | 5,400 | 6,900 | 12,600 | 86,400 |
| Broadcast 21–30 | 60 | 600 | 1,500 | 3,000 | 5,400 | 7,200 | 13,200 | 86,400 |
| Broadcast 31–42 | 60 | 600 | 1,500 | 3,000 | 5,400 | 7,200 | 13,500 | 43,200 |

Viewing sessions can span several broadcasts, and the longest lasts nearly four days. Their duration is not a watch percentage or a program length.

## 4. Data-quality issues

1. **DST rather than an unexplained duration error.** Naive subtraction disagrees with `duraton` in 117 rows, always by exactly +3,600 seconds. All 117 cross `2020-03-29 04:00:00`; no viewing start or stop occurs in local hour 03 that day. `Europe/Kyiv` localization followed by UTC subtraction matches every checked row near the transition (135,487 rows), and the full corrected diagnostic has zero duration mismatches. Across 394 schedule channel transitions, next-start minus current-start minus duration is also exactly 3,600 naive seconds. Example: channel 3, March 29 01:25, duration 6,000, next start 04:05. This strongly supports a skipped local hour, not arbitrary corrupted durations. The precise timezone name remains an inference, since several zones share this transition.
2. **Do not add elapsed seconds on a naive/local wall clock across DST.** Localize schedule start, convert to UTC, then add duration on that UTC timeline; localize both viewing endpoints separately. Keep local calendar boundaries for the week split. Audit both parsed duration consistency and nonexistent/ambiguous times in Step 2.
3. **17 exact duplicate viewing records.** Deduplicate derived data or union intervals; leave originals intact. The 17 rows do not explain all overlap inflation.
4. **Substantial same-user/channel overlap and adjacency.** Unioning 5,821,987 raw intervals yields 5,441,773 segments (this reduction includes touching fragments). Same-channel duplicate/overlap time inflates naive summed elapsed viewing by **116,225,303 seconds**. Fragment counts must not be used as watch-frequency counts.
5. **Concurrent different-channel viewing.** Summed per-user/channel union time is 8,502,989,921 seconds; union across all channels per user is 7,872,180,150 seconds. The 630,809,771-second excess demonstrates concurrency. The files do not identify devices or prove fraud. Keep channel-specific evidence for matching; do not invent a single-device sequence or sum this as unique human attention. Binary user support and qualifying-airing counts reduce duration inflation sensitivity.
6. **Schedule gaps and missing channels.** Five viewed channels (`149, 1174, 1508, 1509, 1510`) are absent from both historical schedules, accounting for 113,579 view rows. Overall, 413,297 view rows have no schedule overlap under the DST-aware interpretation; some are gaps/coverage limitations on otherwise present channels. Do not label those rows as negative feedback or infer a program from a nearby title.
7. **One zero-duration schedule row.** Early file, channel 644, `29.03.2020 04:00:00`, ID 0. Quarantine/drop from derived interval calculations. No negative IDs or other nonpositive intervals were observed; all view intervals are positive.
8. **Schedule overlaps.** The naive per-file check found 2 / 2 / 8 rows overlapping earlier same-channel coverage, with 0 / 0 / 4 labelled-versus-labelled overlaps. Exact duplicate rows within each schedule are zero. Boundary raw-row comparisons across successive files found zero exact duplicates; on historically viewed channels, combined/deduplicated labelled airings had no overlaps under either tested clock interpretation. Still assert this property in the production join; do not silently double-credit conflicting program assignments if encountered. Future-schedule overlaps cannot supply future user labels.
9. **IDs identify recurring programs, not necessarily a unique episode/title string.** Positive IDs with multiple titles: 1,685 / 2,508 / 1,679 per schedule file. Positive IDs with multiple categories within a file: zero. Use IDs as items; choose a documented representative historical title for display. Do not create new items solely from episode title variations.
10. **Nine categories overall, eight among positive IDs.** All categories include `Музыка`; it does not occur among positive-ID rows in these files. Metadata is sparse and some years are ranges. CBF feasibility does not imply useful metadata for every item.
11. **Selection and drift.** All recorded view durations exceed 60 seconds; this is an observed truncation, not a verified competition watched threshold. Weekly volume changes sharply: 105,223 starts in Week 27 versus 271,172 in Week 28. No causal explanation is established. The validation interval has fewer rows and longer overlap durations than training, so use a chronological evaluation and report limitations.

## 5. Missing program ID analysis

| Schedule file | ID 0 rows | Labelled rows | Labelled row share | Labelled share of summed broadcast seconds |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 11–20 | 958,622 | 115,613 | 10.7624% | 15.9663% |
| 21–30 | 952,889 | 121,505 | 11.3092% | 16.9000% |
| 31–42 | 1,150,604 | 144,774 | 11.1762% | 16.6721% |

**Clarification of the exam's shorthand:** “10.8%” is the early-file **row fraction**, not literally the proportion of elapsed airtime. The duration-weighted quantities above are summed row durations, not overlap-corrected channel exposure. The published unique counts include sentinel 0, so recommendable distinct counts are one lower. This explanation refines measured quantities without relaxing the missing-ID requirement.

DST-aware matching of the original view rows gives:

| Match status | Raw view rows |
|---|---:|
| At least one labelled-airing overlap | 2,964,378 |
| Some schedule coverage, but no labelled overlap | 2,444,312 |
| No schedule overlap | 413,297 |
| Total | 5,821,987 |

Thus 50.9169% of view rows touch a labelled airing; 4,497,257,030 of 8,502,989,921 per-user/channel union seconds (52.8903%) intersect labelled airings. User exposure is not uniformly distributed across schedule rows, so 10.8% schedule coverage does not imply only 10.8% of viewing is identifiable.

**Proposed ID policy:** retain ID-0 rows only for coverage/context diagnostics; exclude them from all item catalogs, training edges, support counts, relevance sets, and recommendations. Do not infer a missing ID from title similarity in the mandatory implementation. Missing labels are unknowns, not evidence of dislike. Retain unmatched/no-ID counts so failures can be discussed honestly. Template zeros are placeholders to replace later, not valid output items.

## 6. Viewing-to-program matching design

### Exact rule and double-count prevention

For view interval `V=[v_start,v_stop)` and airing `A=[a_start,a_start+duration)` on the same channel:

```text
vsetv_id == channel_id
overlap_seconds = max(0, min(v_stop, a_end) - max(v_start, a_start))
```

Use half-open intervals: touching endpoints have zero overlap. All interval arithmetic should use UTC elapsed seconds under the documented local-clock interpretation. Merely joining on channel/date or choosing the first broadcast after a view starts is incorrect.

Proposed processing order:

1. Read exact string user IDs; parse both timestamp formats explicitly; check/record the timezone assumption. Reject/quarantine invalid spans without editing originals.
2. Establish training/validation boundaries before any behavior aggregation. Clip viewing time to its period. The 1,007 raw intervals crossing the training cutoff contribute only their pre-cutoff portion to training; remaining time is validation evidence only.
3. Deduplicate schedule airing identity `(channel_id, start_utc, end_utc, tv_show_id)` after comparing metadata; preserve conflict diagnostics. Boundary spillovers from the adjacent historical file can complete availability, but not expand behavior cutoffs.
4. Group view fragments by `(user_id, channel_id)` within the period, union overlapping/touching fragments, then intersect with all eligible labelled airings. This avoids duplicate-time credit while allowing one long session to match multiple programs.
5. Accumulate disjoint overlap pieces for each `(user_id, channel, airing_start, airing_end, tv_show_id, period)` before applying the watched threshold. Two short fragments of the same airing can jointly qualify. Do not add separate repeat broadcasts merely to pass a per-airing threshold.
6. Count qualifying distinct airings for frequency, retain union seconds as an optional weight, and deduplicate `(user_id, program_id)` for binary relevance/support. Check total credited time per user-airing does not exceed its broadcast duration. If overlapping different labelled IDs exist on one channel, quarantine ambiguous time or resolve it explicitly and identically for all methods; historical diagnostics did not encounter this on viewed channels.

# Step 2 — viewing-to-program preprocessing

**Student:** Abaidullah Seikh · **Instructor:** Seungmin Jin  
**Stage:** preprocessing and independent verification only  
**Source of requirements:** completed `results/step1_audit.md` and all 125 lines of `exam_quiz_FKN.md`, read before implementation.

**Outcome:** the complete historical viewing-to-broadcast pipeline ran successfully. The selected 120-second rule produces **716,796 training** and **569,104 validation user–program pairs**, exactly matching Step 1. All **26 current tests** and **100 full-data verification checks** pass. One initial timestamp-validation test failed, was fixed, and remains recorded in the evidence. The original five CSVs and the original Step 1 OpenCode export have unchanged SHA-256 hashes.

The current Step 2 request restricts this milestone to preprocessing; it supersedes the broader implementation sequence proposed in Step 1 §15. Recommendation methods and evaluation remain later milestones. No recommendation models, MAP@5 scores, or Kaggle prediction file were produced.

## Scope and protocol

### Exact schemas and identity preservation

The loader requires the inspected column order and fails on an unexpected header or record width:

- Views: `user_id,vsetv_id,start_time,stop_time,duraton`.
- Schedules: `channel_id,channel_title,start_time,duration,tv_show_title,tv_show_id,tv_show_category,tv_show_genre_1,tv_show_genre_2,tv_show_genre_3,year_of_production,director,actors`.
- Original template: `user_id,tv_show_id`.

User IDs remain original strings from ingestion through SQLite, CSV output, grouping, and coverage checks. No conversion to float or integer is used for user identity. Verification includes IDs above signed-int64 range and distinct strings `000123` and `123`. Consumers of derived CSVs must continue to load `user_id` as text.

### Time interpretation and boundaries

**Europe/Kyiv is an evidence-supported inference, not an officially declared competition timezone.** Viewing timestamps are explicitly parsed as `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS`; schedule starts as `DD.MM.YYYY HH:MM:SS`. Dates and clock fields are validated. Transition-day local times are round-tripped through UTC: nonexistent times are rejected, and ambiguous autumn times require an explicit fold. The supplied periods precede the autumn transition, but that behavior is tested.

Elapsed-time arithmetic uses UTC integer seconds. Broadcast end is **UTC-localized start + elapsed schedule duration**, so adding an hour across the spring clock jump is correct. Viewing endpoints are localized separately, and their elapsed difference must equal the supplied `duraton`. This check succeeded for every source viewing record, including the 117 DST-crossing records identified in Step 1. A cached day offset accelerates ordinary dates; transition dates take the explicit fold/round-trip path.

| Partition | Local half-open interval | UTC Unix-second interval |
|---|---|---|
| Train | `[2020-03-09 00:00, 2020-05-18 00:00)` | `[1583704800, 1589749200)` |
| Validation | `[2020-05-18 00:00, 2020-07-27 00:00)` | `[1589749200, 1595797200)` |
| Full history | `[2020-03-09 00:00, 2020-07-27 00:00)` | `[1583704800, 1595797200)` |
| Test availability only | `[2020-07-27 00:00, 2020-10-19 00:00)` | `[1595797200, 1603054800)` |

Training/validation viewing is clipped separately before matching. A future-only viewing record cannot enter either partition; the integration test inserts one explicitly and verifies its exclusion. Test schedule rows contribute availability IDs only and are never joined to user behavior. Full-history outputs are prepared data for possible later fitting; **they must not be used to train a model being evaluated on the Week 21–30 hold-out**.

### Join, union, and configurable threshold

1. Stream and validate original files; check their hashes against Step 1 before processing and again afterward.
2. Use a disk-backed sort by `(channel,user,start,end,original_record)`. Remove exact duplicate viewing records by their complete original parsed CSV field values. Preserve original files.
3. Within each user/channel and partition, union overlapping or touching viewing intervals. A continuous session may match several broadcasts; distinct channels are not merged into one artificial viewing sequence.
4. Deduplicate broadcast identities `(channel,start_utc,end_utc,program_id)` in the channel index. Invalid zero-duration broadcasts are excluded. Conflicting overlapping positive-ID airings on a viewed historical channel cause a clear failure rather than silent double credit; none occurred in this run.
5. Match only the same channel and positive half-open interval overlap:

   `max(0, min(view_end,broadcast_end) - max(view_start,broadcast_start))`.

6. Sum disjoint matching fragments **per user and broadcast** before deciding whether it was watched. Keep the threshold-independent seconds and first/last matched timestamps on disk, including overlaps shorter than 120 seconds.
7. Combine the two disjoint partitions' raw per-broadcast overlaps to form full history **before thresholding**. This is not concatenation of thresholded training and validation tables.
8. Derive user–program pairs by keeping broadcasts whose summed overlap is at least the requested threshold, then aggregating qualifying-broadcast counts, credited seconds, and first/last qualifying watch times for each user and program.

The selected threshold is **120 elapsed seconds per user/broadcast**, configured with `--threshold-seconds 120`. It is the Step 1 evidence-based starting rule, not a universal watched definition or a verified hidden Kaggle label rule. A second **300-second** dataset was actually derived from the same saved overlap cache. No raw interval join was rebuilt for that alternative. Different airings of the same program cannot pool subthreshold seconds to pass the per-broadcast cutoff.

## Implementation and derived outputs

### Source and verification files

| File | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `code/data_pipeline.py` | Production ingestion, explicit timezone parsing, exact deduplication, union, interval index, threshold-free join, and separate threshold derivation CLI |
| `code/test_data_pipeline.py` | Unit/integration suite and independent brute-force reference |
| `code/verify_step2.py` | Full-output invariants, independent SQL aggregation, history-merge check, Step 1 comparison, source/session integrity |
| `tests/interval_fixtures.json` | Eleven hand-specified fixtures with exact expected overlap records |
| `tests/run_step2_tests.sh` | Test entry point: `sh tests/run_step2_tests.sh` |
| `results/step2_test_runs/run_001.json` | Initial test attempt, including the real failed assertion |
| `results/step2_test_runs/run_002.json` | Corrected parser suite, all passing |
| `results/step2_test_runs/run_003.json` | Final suite after moving temporary test files under the project, all passing |
| `results/step2_verification.json` | Passed/failed full checks, all test attempts, output statistics, hashes, comparison deltas, timing and memory |
| `results/step2_preprocessing_report.md` | This report |

All Python implementation and test code is inside `code/`. `tests/` contains the executable shell entry point, fixtures, and documentation, satisfying the requested test directory while preserving the all-Python-in-`code/` requirement. The root, data, tests, and dependency documentation were updated for this stage.

    train_airing_overlaps.csv.gz

    history_airing_overlaps.csv.gz

**Threshold-free overlap schema:**

`user_id,channel_id,broadcast_start_utc,broadcast_end_utc,tv_show_id,overlap_seconds,first_overlap_utc,last_overlap_utc`.

One row represents a user and one airing within one partition, with positive unioned seconds. 246: Avoid a Cartesian DataFrame join. Channel-sorted interval sweeps or start-time/prefix-max-end indexes plus bounded search are feasible. The inspection used SQLite ordering and per-channel interval indexes, not an exported interaction training set.
247: 
248: ### Observed overlap distribution
249: 
250: The following are full-data descriptive join measurements under the supported `Europe/Kyiv` hypothesis, not samples or model results. “User-airing union” sums only disjoint fragments of that specific broadcast within the period. Quantiles are nearest-rank.
251: 
252: | Population | Count | P10 (s) | P25 | Median | P75 | P90 | P99 | Max |
253: |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
254: | Train raw-view × labelled-airing overlaps | 2,383,336 | 77 | 146 | 465 | 1,322 | 2,782 | 6,577 | 22,800 |
255: | Train user-airing union overlaps | 1,823,893 | 86 | 197 | 621 | 1,767 | 3,599 | 7,253 | 28,387 |
256: | Validation raw-view × airing overlaps | 1,465,129 | 83 | 174 | 600 | 1,803 | 4,262 | 8,100 | 30,000 |
257: | Validation user-airing union overlaps | 1,191,015 | 95 | 245 | 888 | 2,508 | 5,134 | 8,700 | 30,000 |
258: 
259: Constructed user-airing watched fractions, `union_overlap / full_broadcast_duration`: training P25 **4.10%**, median **17.27%**, P75 **57.74%**; validation P25 **4.89%**, median **23.83%**, P75 **79.25%**. Fractions were stored to one basis point for diagnostics; a rounded zero does not mean an actual zero-length intersection. At least the 90th percentile is 100% in each period. There is no pre-existing watch-percentage column.
260: 
261: ### Proposed watched threshold: 120 elapsed seconds per user-airing
262: 
263: | Absolute cutoff | Qualifying train user-airings | Train users | Qualifying validation user-airings | Validation users |
264: |---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
265: | ≥60 s | 1,773,566 | 4,841 | 1,165,285 | 4,806 |
266: | **≥120 s** | **1,531,876** | **4,837** | **1,028,093** | **4,804** |
267: | ≥300 s | 1,224,147 | 4,833 | 855,420 | 4,799 |
268: | ≥600 s | 958,577 | 4,824 | 707,790 | 4,792 |
269: 
270: **Rationale from training data:** 120 seconds excludes very brief/boundary overlaps while retaining **83.99%** of positive user-airing overlaps. A 300-second rule retains only **67.12%** and excludes all programs shorter than five minutes. The 120-second rule still excludes broadcasts shorter than two minutes; this is an explicit limitation. A high percentage threshold would also penalize long broadcasts even where absolute viewing is substantial. Choose the simple absolute cutoff as the initial frozen protocol; do not claim it reproduces Kaggle's hidden label construction or is empirically optimal.
271: 
272: The validation threshold table is a coverage audit, not label tuning for a favorable score. If later comparing thresholds or a fraction rule, name each protocol separately and rerun every method with that protocol; never compare methods evaluated against different relevance definitions as if the scores were commensurate.
273: 
274: ## 7. MAP@5 definition
275: 
276: **Confirmed from the exam:** metric is MAP@K, higher is better, and this exam fixes K=5. **Confirmed from presentation pp.4–5:** normalize each user's AP by `min(K, |R_u|)`, then macro-average across users. The slides explicitly say to match the evaluator convention. The detailed live Kaggle scorer implementation was not retrievable, so empty-label/duplicate-prediction behavior and hidden relevance construction remain unconfirmed by the platform.
277: 
278: For the proposed local protocol, let `R_u` be the set of distinct positive program IDs with a qualifying validation airing, and `p_u[1:5]` the ordered predictions. Define `hit_u(r)=1` only for a relevant ID's first appearance; otherwise 0. Then:
279: 
280: ```text
281: P_u@r  = (sum_{j=1..r} hit_u(j)) / r
282: AP_u@5 = (sum_{r=1..5} P_u@r * hit_u(r)) / min(5, |R_u|), when |R_u| > 0
283: MAP@5  = (1 / |U|) * sum_{u in U} AP_u@5
284: ```
285: 
286: **Proposed edge policies:** empty `R_u` gives AP=0 for the primary all-user metric; duplicate predicted IDs cannot earn repeated hits and are rejected by the output validator; exactly five unique positive eligible IDs are required. Macro-average users, not views, and do not divide by the number of retrieved hits or by five when fewer than five relevant items exist.
287: 
288: The presentation's example is a useful future unit-test target: relevant `{A,B,C}`, ranking `A,B,D,C,E` gives `(1+1+3/4)/3 = 11/12`; `D,A,E,B,C` gives `(1/2+2/4+3/5)/3 = 8/15`. These are illustrative arithmetic examples, **not project experiment results or student personal verification**.
289: 
290: The slide's competition screenshot describes “five most preferred” programs from future viewing. It does not reveal how preference was computed or how many ground-truth IDs the scorer retains. Our proposed “any ≥120-second qualifying airing” relevance set is therefore a transparent offline proxy, not a verified recreation of private labels. Do not claim public/private MAP equivalence based on the metric formula alone.
291: 
292: ## 8. Temporal validation protocol
293: 
294: ### Fixed chronological periods
295: 
296: Use local calendar ISO-week boundaries, then convert to UTC for arithmetic:
297: 
298: | Role | Local half-open interval | Actual evidence and permitted behavior |
299: |---|---|---|
300: | Training, Weeks 11–20 | `[2020-03-09 00:00:00, 2020-05-18 00:00:00)` | 3,945,173 view rows touch training; fit all model statistics only here. |
301: | Validation, Weeks 21–30 | `[2020-05-18 00:00:00, 2020-07-27 00:00:00)` | 1,877,821 view rows touch validation, including the post-cutoff portion of 1,007 boundary-crossing rows. Labels/selection only. |
302: | Final fitting, Weeks 11–30 | `[2020-03-09 00:00:00, 2020-07-27 00:00:00)` | Refit chosen, frozen strategy using all available historical behavior only after comparison/selection. |
303: | Test prediction, Weeks 31–42 | `[2020-07-27 00:00:00, 2020-10-19 00:00:00)` | Use schedule for availability; no test viewing is available or permitted. Exclude Week 43 spillover. |

305: Under the Kyiv interpretation the UTC boundaries are March 8 22:00, May 17 21:00, July 26 21:00, and October 18 21:00 respectively. The training interval crosses DST, so fixed-offset conversion for the entire period is wrong. The two raw-row period counts sum to the full view count plus 1,007 because clipping splits crossing intervals, not because those seconds should be counted twice.
306: 
307: ### Shared comparison contract (proposal)
308: 
309: - **Fit population:** all users with permitted training history, not just the test-template users. No validation history may create popularity counts, co-view edges, rules, user profiles, recency features, or hyperparameter-specific fitted statistics.
310: - **Primary evaluation users:** exactly the **1,260 original template users**, preserved as strings and in original order. This mirrors the known target cohort and keeps users fixed independently of model capability. Do not drop cold users to improve a score.
311: - **Relevance:** distinct positive IDs from ≥120 seconds of unioned overlap with at least one validation airing. No artificial truncation to five relevant items without confirmation of the hidden label rule.
312: - **Primary MAP:** all 1,260 users, empty relevance → AP=0. There are **1,246 nonempty-label users** and **14 empty-label users**. Report the count and also a clearly labelled nonempty-only MAP diagnostic for those same 1,246 users. The all-user theoretical ceiling from empty rows alone is 1,246/1,260 = 0.988889, not an achieved score.
313: - **Train history coverage:** 4,876 users have any training viewing; 4,837 have a ≥120-second labelled airing. Among template users, 1,256 have any training viewing and 1,250 have qualifying history: **10 cold users**, comprising four with no training viewing and six with viewing but no usable labelled overlap. Eight of the ten have nonempty validation relevance.
314: - **Final cold cases:** two template users have no ≥120-second labelled airing in either historical partition. Their histories require the shared fallback. This is a coverage diagnostic, not a final-model fitting result.
315: - **Common candidates, repeats, tie-breaking, fallback:** as in §9 for every method.
316: - **Selection:** a small predeclared hyperparameter grid, one common hold-out, all attempted comparisons retained. Select with MAP@5 and documented compute/coverage tradeoffs. Validation guides selection, never the fitted model's user-item statistics. Multiple trials on one hold-out are subject to selection optimism; disclose that limitation.
317: - **Final refit:** rebuild interactions over the entire history window, including recombining any airing fragments split by the now-removed validation boundary. Do not blindly concatenate thresholded train/validation tables, which could miss a boundary airing qualifying only in combination.
318: - Choose the same heavy and light/cold users from training-only history descriptors, with a deterministic rule and justification before looking for flattering recommendation examples. Compare their eventual lists against validation behavior, not inaccessible test outcomes.

### Proposed watched threshold: 120 elapsed seconds per user-airing

| Absolute cutoff | Qualifying train user-airings | Train users | Qualifying validation user-airings | Validation users |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| ≥60 s | 1,773,566 | 4,841 | 1,165,285 | 4,806 |
| **≥120 s** | **1,531,876** | **4,837** | **1,028,093** | **4,804** |
| ≥300 s | 1,224,147 | 4,833 | 855,420 | 4,799 |
| ≥600 s | 958,577 | 4,824 | 707,790 | 4,792 |

**Rationale from training data:** 120 seconds excludes very brief/boundary overlaps while retaining **83.99%** of positive user-airing overlaps. A 300-second rule retains only **67.12%** and excludes all programs shorter than five minutes. The 120-second rule still excludes broadcasts shorter than two minutes; this is an explicit limitation. A high percentage threshold would also penalize long broadcasts even where absolute viewing is substantial. Choose the simple absolute cutoff as the initial frozen protocol; do not claim it reproduces Kaggle's hidden label construction or is empirically optimal.

The validation threshold table is a coverage audit, not label tuning for a favorable score. If later comparing thresholds or a fraction rule, name each protocol separately and rerun every method with that protocol; never compare methods evaluated against different relevance definitions as if the scores were commensurate.

## 7. MAP@5 definition

**Confirmed from the exam:** metric is MAP@K, higher is better, and this exam fixes K=5. **Confirmed from presentation pp.4–5:** normalize each user's AP by `min(K, |R_u|)`, then macro-average across users. The slides explicitly say to match the evaluator convention. The detailed live Kaggle scorer implementation was not retrievable, so empty-label/duplicate-prediction behavior and hidden relevance construction remain unconfirmed by the platform.

For the proposed local protocol, let `R_u` be the set of distinct positive program IDs with a qualifying validation airing, and `p_u[1:5]` the ordered predictions. Define `hit_u(r)=1` only for a relevant ID's first appearance; otherwise 0. Then:

```text
P_u@r  = (sum_{j=1..r} hit_u(j)) / r
AP_u@5 = (sum_{r=1..5} P_u@r * hit_u(r)) / min(5, |R_u|), when |R_u| > 0
MAP@5  = (1 / |U|) * sum_{u in U} AP_u@5
```

**Proposed edge policies:** empty `R_u` gives AP=0 for the primary all-user metric; duplicate predicted IDs cannot earn repeated hits and are rejected by the output validator; exactly five unique positive eligible IDs are required. Macro-average users, not views, and do not divide by the number of retrieved hits or by five when fewer than five relevant items exist.

The presentation's example is a useful future unit-test target: relevant `{A,B,C}`, ranking `A,B,D,C,E` gives `(1+1+3/4)/3 = 11/12`; `D,A,E,B,C` gives `(1/2+2/4+3/5)/3 = 8/15`. These are illustrative arithmetic examples, **not project experiment results or student personal verification**.

The slide's competition screenshot describes “five most preferred” programs from future viewing. It does not reveal how preference was computed or how many ground-truth IDs the scorer retains. Our proposed “any ≥120-second qualifying airing” relevance set is therefore a transparent offline proxy, not a verified recreation of private labels. Do not claim public/private MAP equivalence based on the metric formula alone.

| Role | Local half-open interval | Actual evidence and permitted behavior |
|---|---|---|

### Shared comparison contract (proposal)

- **Fit population:** all users with permitted training history, not just the test-template users. No validation history may create popularity counts, co-view edges, rules, user profiles, recency features, or hyperparameter-specific fitted statistics.
- **Primary evaluation users:** exactly the **1,260 original template users**, preserved as strings and in original order. This mirrors the known target cohort and keeps users fixed independently of model capability. Do not drop cold users to improve a score.
- **Relevance:** distinct positive IDs from ≥120 seconds of unioned overlap with at least one validation airing. No artificial truncation to five relevant items without confirmation of the hidden label rule.
- **Primary MAP:** all 1,260 users, empty relevance → AP=0. There are **1,246 nonempty-label users** and **14 empty-label users**. Report the count and also a clearly labelled nonempty-only MAP diagnostic for those same 1,246 users. The all-user theoretical ceiling from empty rows alone is 1,246/1,260 = 0.988889, not an achieved score.
- **Train history coverage:** 4,876 users have any training viewing; 4,837 have a ≥120-second labelled airing. Among template users, 1,256 have any training viewing and 1,250 have qualifying history: **10 cold users**, comprising four with no training viewing and six with viewing but no usable labelled overlap. Eight of the ten have nonempty validation relevance.
- **Final cold cases:** two template users have no ≥120-second labelled airing in either historical partition. Their histories require the shared fallback. This is a coverage diagnostic, not a final-model fitting result.
- **Common candidates, repeats, tie-breaking, fallback:** as in §9 for every method.
- **Selection:** a small predeclared hyperparameter grid, one common hold-out, all attempted comparisons retained. Select with MAP@5 and documented compute/coverage tradeoffs. Validation guides selection, never the fitted model's user-item statistics. Multiple trials on one hold-out are subject to selection optimism; disclose that limitation.
- **Final refit:** rebuild interactions over the entire history window, including recombining any airing fragments split by the now-removed validation boundary. Do not blindly concatenate thresholded train/validation tables, which could miss a boundary airing qualifying only in combination.
- Choose the same heavy and light/cold users from training-only history descriptors, with a deterministic rule and justification before looking for flattering recommendation examples. Compare their eventual lists against validation behavior, not inaccessible test outcomes.

## 9. Candidate-pool and cold-start policy

**Proposal:** include all positive program IDs having a valid airing with positive overlap with the prediction window. Use actual airing timestamps across adjacent schedule files, not merely the filename of the target schedule. Only the availability catalog may look ahead; learned user behavior may not.

| Timestamp-clipped catalog | Positive IDs |
|---|---:|
| Training-window schedule | 5,842 |
| Validation-window schedule | 6,384 |
| Test-window schedule | 6,649 |

The validation catalog has **2,391** IDs absent from the training-window schedule; test has **1,436** absent from the historical-window catalogs. Counts exceed the corresponding single-file counts where preceding-file spillovers genuinely air within the window. This is a proposed inclusive availability policy, not a claim Kaggle enforces this exact catalog. The scan used schedule metadata only; no future behavior was consulted.

**Allow previously watched programs for every method.** The exam does not forbid them. Among template users' 198,517 distinct validation user-program pairs at 120 seconds, 42,934 (21.63%) also occur in the same user's training history. This supports treating repeat consumption as possible; it is not a measured recommendation gain. “Allow repeats” means across time, not duplicate IDs inside one Top-5.

**Common fallback order, determined from training only:** candidate programs by descending distinct training-user support, then descending qualifying-airing count, then ascending numeric program ID. Cold items receive zero learned support and appear only after supported items unless a later individually evaluated method can score them. If all candidate supports are zero, deterministic ID ordering still provides five eligible IDs; no unrecorded random or future-popularity fallback is allowed.

**For every method:** filter IDs to the shared candidate catalog; remove 0 and duplicates; rank by method score with the same fallback ordering for ties; keep up to five positively supported method recommendations; fill missing slots from the common fallback without duplication. If a user lacks usable seeds/rules/graph reachability, return that fallback. Assert that at least five candidates exist; observed catalogs comfortably satisfy this. Do not treat independently scaled model scores as probabilities.

**Cold-item limitation:** the training inspection sees only 2,948 watched program IDs despite 5,842 scheduled candidates. Pure history, PPR, and rules cannot learn behavior for unseen items. This limits coverage and motivates later CBF exploration, but does not justify silently narrowing other methods' candidate pools.

## 10. Recommended algorithms

Implement the four planned methods in this order. The two qualifying exam methods are **program co-view PPR and Association Rules**. No method has been evaluated, and no performance claim is made.

| Priority | Method | Proposed definition | Feasibility and limitations |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Required popularity baseline | Distinct training users with qualifying program viewing; common tie/fallback rule | One pass over deduplicated user-item presence. Essential reference; not one of the two approved methods. |
| 2 | Personal viewing frequency | Per-user count of distinct qualifying broadcasts of each ID, then shared fallback | Sparse lookup and ranking. Do not count raw fragments or conflate it with approved CF/MF. |
| 3 | Personalized PageRank | Nodes are program IDs; weighted **program–program co-view** edges built from training users; restart distribution from that user's qualifying history | Meets the specified graph requirement. Avoid replacing it with user-user PageRank or a popularity-only random walk. |
| 4 | Association Rules | Training user baskets, singleton antecedent/consequent rules `i→j` with support, confidence, lift | Approved method. Length-two itemsets keep computation bounded; this is a documented restricted rule-mining design, not a claim of full Apriori/FP-Growth enumeration. |

### PPR specification to implement, not an executed experiment

- Binary training incidence `X[u,i]`; integer co-view counts from `X.T @ X`, diagonal removed. Use at least int32 for counts, not uint8 multiplication that can overflow.
- Initial edge weight proposal: cosine-normalized co-user support `co_count(i,j)/sqrt(support(i)*support(j))`; require at least three co-view users; retain top 100 neighbors per item, symmetrize explicitly, then row-normalize. Deterministic tie handling.
- Personalized restart `s_u(i) ∝ log1p(qualifying_airing_count[u,i])` over training history. Initial damping α=0.85; dangling mass returns to `s_u`; iterate `p_next = α P.T p + (1−α)s_u` with the corresponding dangling correction.
- Initial convergence settings: L1 tolerance `1e-8`, maximum 200 iterations, record convergence and wall time. Candidate restriction applies at ranking time, not by deleting all historical seed nodes from the graph. If seeds lack graph edges, use the documented dangling/fallback policy.
- Small planned sensitivity grid: α in `{0.70,0.85}`, neighbor cap in `{50,100}` with other preprocessing fixed. All are untested configuration proposals.

### Association-rule specification to implement

- A basket is a user's distinct qualifying programs in the training window; each user contributes once to a pair's support. Define `N` as the 4,837 nonempty training baskets under the proposed threshold, recomputed by the production pipeline.
- For pair count `n_ij`, `support=n_ij/N`, `confidence(i→j)=n_ij/n_i`, `lift=confidence/(n_j/N)`.
- Initial rule filters: pair count ≥3, confidence ≥0.05, lift ≥1. Score a candidate by the sum over watched antecedents of normalized user-history weight × confidence × `log1p(lift)`; retain explanatory antecedents. A simple confidence-only alternative may be a separately logged ablation.
- Candidate repeats remain permitted. Missing rules or fewer than five supported consequents use the exact shared fallback, not a special model-only policy. A small support-count grid `{3,5,10}` is sufficient initially; avoid exhaustive hyperparameter search before correctness checks.

### Scale, memory, runtime

The DST-aware 120-second audit found **716,796 training user-program pairs**, 4,837 nonempty users, and 2,948 watched items. Median user basket: 132 items; maximum: 1,171. Enumerating every user's unordered pair would emit **76,705,132 pair occurrences** before aggregation. A Python dictionary of every event/pair is unnecessary; sparse integer multiplication or streamed pair accumulation is preferable. Both PPR and rules may reuse training-only co-view statistics while retaining different, independently evaluated scoring mechanisms.

Array-storage estimates, not measured model memory:
- Training CSR with float32 values/int32 indices is roughly **5.49 MiB** excluding maps, intermediates, and overhead.
- A dense 2,948² float32 item matrix is **33.15 MiB**; an 8,234² matrix is **258.63 MiB**. Dense co-occurrence intermediate storage is possible at this scale but sparse/pruned graphs give better headroom.
- A directed top-100 graph over 8,234 items needs about 6.3 MiB for value/index arrays before symmetrization and overhead. Batch PPR by 32–64 users to bound workspace. A Python-object graph can consume much more memory than arrays.
- Preprocessing diagnostics actually took minutes (§11). PPR cost is approximately `O(users × iterations × graph_edges)` without batching/reuse; rules' main cost is pair aggregation. Model wall times are **not measured yet**. Benchmark the initial configuration and cap grids before expanding scope.

**Dependencies:** NumPy/SciPy for sparse arrays and numerical operations, pytest for meaningful verification; NetworkX could be a tiny-graph reference but is not installed and is not needed for the production graph. `mlxtend` is optional for a small rule-check reference, not necessary for pair rules. All are currently uninstalled in the inspected interpreter.

**Defer until the mandatory comparison is verified:** CBF (sparse metadata and missing years), implicit MF/ALS (additional library/Python compatibility and hyperparameters), hybrids (evaluate individual components first; rank fusion avoids pretending raw scores are comparable). Do not create unused algorithm files now. The current diagnostic code uses only the standard library and no copied participant code.

## 13. Gate 0 risks

76: def stable_day_offset(day):

80:     has no same-day pair of offset transitions; no fixed offset is used globally.

84:                for h in (0, 12, 24)}

88: def parse_timestamp(value, schedule=False, fold=None):
89:     pattern = SCHEDULE_PATTERN if schedule else VIEW_PATTERN
90:     if not pattern.fullmatch(value):
91:         raise ValueError(f"Unexpected timestamp format: {value!r}")
92:     if not (0 <= int(value[11:13]) < 24 and 0 <= int(value[14:16]) < 60
93:             and 0 <= int(value[17:19]) < 60):
94:         raise ValueError(f"Out-of-range clock fields: {value!r}")
95:     if fold not in (None, 0, 1):
96:         raise ValueError("Invalid fold")
97:     text = value[6:10] + "-" + value[3:5] + "-" + value[:2] + value[10:] if schedule else value
98:     naive = datetime.fromisoformat(text)
99:     offset = stable_day_offset(naive.date())
100:     if offset is not None:
101:         return int((naive - EPOCH).total_seconds()) - offset
102:     options = {}
103:     for candidate_fold in (0, 1):
104:         aware = naive.replace(tzinfo=ZONE, fold=candidate_fold)
105:         utc = aware.astimezone(timezone.utc)
106:         if utc.astimezone(ZONE).replace(tzinfo=None) == naive:
107:             options[candidate_fold] = int(utc.timestamp())
108:     if not options:

152: def union_intervals(spans, window=None):

170: class AiringIndex:

173:     def __init__(self, airings):

188: def match_channel(spans, index, window):
189:     """Optimized interval join; accumulate fragments before applying ANY threshold."""
190:     totals = {}
191:     for start, end in union_intervals(spans, window):
192:         left, right = bisect_right(index.ends, start), bisect_left(index.starts, end)
193:         for i in range(left, right):
194:             airing = index.airings[i]
195:             first, last = max(start, airing.start), min(end, airing.end)
196:             if first < last:

198:                 totals[airing] = Overlap(last - first + (old.seconds if old else 0),
199:                                         min(old.first, first) if old else first,
200:                                         max(old.last, last) if old else last)

203:                 and window[0] <= value.first < value.last <= window[1]):
204:             raise AssertionError("Invalid credited seconds or temporal leakage")

236: class CoverageIndex:

239:     def __init__(self, spans):
240:         merged = union_intervals(spans)
241:         self.starts = [s for s, _ in merged]
242:         self.ends = [e for _, e in merged]
243:         self.prefix = [0]
244:         for s, e in merged:
245:             self.prefix.append(self.prefix[-1] + e - s)

247:     def seconds(self, start, end):
248:         left, right = bisect_right(self.ends, start), bisect_left(self.starts, end)
249:         if left >= right:
250:             return 0
251:         return (self.prefix[right] - self.prefix[left]
252:                 - max(0, start - self.starts[left]) - max(0, self.ends[right - 1] - end))

+"""FKN AP@5/MAP@5, strict prediction validation, and fallback consumption only.
+
+No recommendation method or popularity statistics are fitted in this module.
+User keys are exact strings. Program tokens are canonical positive decimal IDs;
+Python ints are accepted losslessly, but floats, bools and normalized text are not.
+"""
+
+from collections.abc import Mapping
+from dataclasses import dataclass
+import hashlib
+import json
+import math
+
+K = 5
+FALLBACK_POLICY = "distinct_training_users_desc,qualifying_airings_desc,numeric_program_id_asc"
+
+
+def program_id(value):
+    if type(value) is int and value > 0:
+        return str(value)
+    if (type(value) is str and value.isascii() and value.isdecimal()
+            and value[0] != "0"):
+        return value
+    raise ValueError(f"Not a canonical positive program ID: {value!r}")
+
+
+def user_id(value):
+    if type(value) is not str or not value or not value.isascii() or not value.isdecimal():
+        raise ValueError("User IDs must be unchanged decimal strings")
+    return value
+
+
+def ordered_cohort(values):
+    if not isinstance(values, (list, tuple)) or not values:
+        raise ValueError("A nonempty ordered cohort is required")
+    result = tuple(user_id(u) for u in values)
+    if len(set(result)) != len(result):
+        raise ValueError("Duplicate cohort user")
+    return result
+
+
+def candidate_pool(values):
+    values = tuple(program_id(v) for v in values)
+    if len(values) != len(set(values)):
+        raise ValueError("Duplicate candidate ID")
+    return tuple(sorted(values, key=int))
+
+
+def identity_hash(values):
+    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(list(values), separators=(",", ":"), ensure_ascii=True).encode()).hexdigest()
+
+
+def strict_top5(predictions, candidates):
+    if not isinstance(predictions, (list, tuple)) or len(predictions) != K:
+        raise ValueError("Production predictions must be an ordered list of exactly five IDs")
+    if candidates is None:
+        raise ValueError("Strict evaluation requires an eligible candidate pool")
+    items = tuple(program_id(p) for p in predictions)
+    if len(set(items)) != K:
+        raise ValueError("Duplicate recommendation ID")
+    if any(p not in candidates for p in items):
+        raise ValueError("Unknown or unavailable program ID")
+    return items
+
+
+def average_precision_at_5(relevant, predictions, *, strict=False, candidates=None):
+    """AP denominator=min(5, unique relevant items); empty relevance gives zero.
+
+    Non-strict mathematical mode allows short/empty/duplicate rankings. Invalid
+    or ineligible tokens receive no credit and still consume their original rank.
+    Only the first five positions are scored. Production callers use strict=True.
+    """
+    if isinstance(relevant, (str, bytes)) or not isinstance(predictions, (list, tuple)):
+        raise ValueError("Relevance must be a collection and predictions must be ordered")
+    truth = {program_id(p) for p in relevant}
+    eligible = None if candidates is None else {program_id(p) for p in candidates}
+    if eligible is not None and not truth.issubset(eligible):
+        raise ValueError("Ground truth contains an ineligible ID")
+    if strict:
+        predictions = strict_top5(predictions, eligible)
+    seen, hits, contributions = set(), 0, []
+    for rank, raw in enumerate(predictions[:K], 1):
+        try:
+            item = program_id(raw)
+        except ValueError:
+            if strict:
+                raise
+            continue
+        if item in seen:
+            continue
+        seen.add(item)
+        if item in truth and (eligible is None or item in eligible):
+            hits += 1
+            contributions.append(hits / rank)
+    return math.fsum(contributions) / min(K, len(truth)) if truth else 0.0
+
+
+def evaluate_predictions(predictions, truth, cohort, candidates, *, strict=True):
+    """Return primary all-user MAP, separate nonempty diagnostic, and ordered APs."""
+    cohort = ordered_cohort(cohort)
+    eligible = frozenset(candidate_pool(candidates))
+    if not isinstance(predictions, Mapping) or not isinstance(truth, Mapping):
+        raise ValueError("Predictions and truth must be user-keyed mappings")
+    for mapping in (predictions, truth):
+        for u in mapping:
+            user_id(u)
+    cohort_set = set(cohort)
+    if set(truth) != cohort_set:
+        raise ValueError("Truth must explicitly contain every cohort user, including empty labels")
+    if set(predictions) - cohort_set or (strict and set(predictions) != cohort_set):
+        raise ValueError("Prediction cohort mismatch or missing user")
+    per_user, labelled = {}, []
+    for u in cohort:
+        # Validate even empty-label users' predictions; invalid rows never hide behind AP=0.
+        labels = tuple(program_id(p) for p in truth[u])
+        ap = average_precision_at_5(labels, predictions.get(u, []), strict=strict, candidates=eligible)
+        per_user[u] = ap
+        if labels:
+            labelled.append(ap)
+    return {"primary_map_at_5": math.fsum(per_user.values()) / len(cohort),
+            "diagnostic_map_at_5_nonempty": math.fsum(labelled) / len(labelled) if labelled else None,
+            "per_user_ap_at_5": per_user, "primary_users": len(cohort),
+            "nonempty_users": len(labelled), "empty_users": len(cohort) - len(labelled),
+            "mode": "strict_production" if strict else "lenient_math_diagnostic",
+            "cohort_order_sha256": identity_hash(cohort),
+            "candidate_ids_sha256": identity_hash(sorted(eligible, key=int))}
+
+
+def parse_prediction_records(records):
+    """Parse exact two-field CSV-style records without losing duplicate user rows."""
+    result = {}
+    for row in records:
+        if not isinstance(row, Mapping) or set(row) != {"user_id", "tv_show_id"}:
+            raise ValueError("Prediction record must have exactly user_id,tv_show_id")
+        u = user_id(row["user_id"])
+        value = row["tv_show_id"]
+        if u in result or type(value) is not str:
+            raise ValueError("Duplicate user or malformed prediction field")
+        tokens = value.split(" ")
+        if len(tokens) != K:
+            raise ValueError("Exactly five single-space-separated tokens required")
+        items = tuple(program_id(t) for t in tokens)
+        if len(set(items)) != K:
+            raise ValueError("Duplicate recommendation ID")
+        result[u] = items
+    return result
+
+
+@dataclass(frozen=True)
+class FallbackRanking:
+    """Step 4 will supply this training-only ranking; Step 3 only consumes it.
+
+    Provenance assertions prevent accidental split/catalog mismatch. They do not
+    establish that a future model honestly computed its statistics; verify that
+    fitting implementation when it exists. No method to fit a ranking is provided.
+    """
+
+    program_ids: tuple
+    training_sha256: str
+    training_window_utc: tuple
+    candidate_ids_sha256: str
+    policy: str = FALLBACK_POLICY
+
+
+def complete_top5(ranked_ids, fallback, candidates, *, training_sha256, training_window_utc):
+    """Shared deterministic completion; requires an externally supplied fallback."""
+    pool = candidate_pool(candidates)
+    if len(pool) < K or not isinstance(ranked_ids, (tuple, list)):
+        raise ValueError("Need five candidates and an ordered ranking")
+    if not isinstance(fallback, FallbackRanking):
+        raise ValueError("A provenance-tagged fallback ranking is required")
+    if (fallback.training_sha256 != training_sha256
+            or tuple(fallback.training_window_utc) != tuple(training_window_utc)
+            or fallback.candidate_ids_sha256 != identity_hash(pool)
+            or fallback.policy != FALLBACK_POLICY):
+        raise ValueError("Fallback training/catalog provenance mismatch")
+    order = tuple(program_id(p) for p in fallback.program_ids)
+    if len(set(order)) != len(order) or set(order) != set(pool):
+        raise ValueError("Fallback must rank every eligible candidate exactly once")
+    allowed, seen, result = set(pool), set(), []
+    for raw in (*ranked_ids, *order):
+        item = program_id(raw)
+        if item in allowed and item not in seen:
+            result.append(item)
+            seen.add(item)
+        if len(result) == K:
+            return tuple(result)
+    raise AssertionError("Unable to complete five eligible IDs")
*** End Patch

+def reference_ap(relevant, predictions):
+    """Independent exact arithmetic: find each relevant item's first rank.
+
+    Unlike production's running hit counter, this iterates relevant items and
+    recomputes the distinct relevant prefix for their first appearance.
+    Synthetic integer/string tokens only; no production helpers are reused.
+    """
+    truth = set(map(str, relevant))
+    ranking = list(map(str, predictions[:5]))
+    total = Fraction(0)
+    for item in truth:
+        if item in ranking:
+            rank = ranking.index(item) + 1
+            prefix_hits = len(truth.intersection(set(ranking[:rank])))
+            total += Fraction(prefix_hits, rank)
+    return total / min(5, len(truth)) if truth else Fraction(0)

+def reference_ap(relevant, predictions):
+    """Independent exact arithmetic: find each relevant item's first rank.
+
+    Unlike production's running hit counter, this iterates relevant items and
+    recomputes the distinct relevant prefix for their first appearance.
+    Synthetic integer/string tokens only; no production helpers are reused.
+    """
+    truth = set(map(str, relevant))
+    ranking = list(map(str, predictions[:5]))
+    total = Fraction(0)
+    for item in truth:
+        if item in ranking:
+            rank = ranking.index(item) + 1
+            prefix_hits = len(truth.intersection(set(ranking[:rank])))
+            total += Fraction(prefix_hits, rank)
+    return total / min(5, len(truth)) if truth else Fraction(0)

@@
 # Step 3 — MAP@5 and temporal validation
 
+**Student:** Abaidullah Seikh · **Course:** LLM4Rec — Final Exam (FKN)  
+**Scope:** evaluator, fixed validation protocol, candidate verification, and reusable fallback interface. No recommendation model was implemented or fitted, and no Kaggle output was generated.
+
+**Outcome:** **34 automated tests passed**, followed by **110 full-data/contract/integrity checks passed, zero current failures**. The frozen cohort contains **1,260 users**, including **1,246 with labels**, **14 without labels**, and **10 without qualifying training history**. Validation has **6,384 eligible programs**. The framework is ready for Step 4 under the explicitly documented local-label and timezone assumptions.
+
+The seven required documents/code/manifests were read completely before implementation. The compressed files' real headers and sample records were inspected and saved before use. Completed Step 2 preprocessing was neither rerun nor modified.
+
 ## Fixed evaluation protocol
+
+The primary protocol is selected before any recommendation-method evaluation:
+
+| Decision | Frozen policy |
+|---|---|
+| Ranking length | Exactly five unique eligible IDs in production evaluation |
+| Primary population | All 1,260 original template users, in original order |
+| Relevance | All distinct positive program IDs with at least one qualifying validation-period airing |
+| Watched threshold | Existing Step 2 rule: at least 120 elapsed unioned viewing seconds per user/broadcast |
+| AP normalization | `min(5, number of distinct relevant programs)` |
+| Empty-label users | AP@5 = 0, retained in primary MAP |
+| Secondary diagnostic | Macro MAP over the same cohort's 1,246 nonempty-label users |
+| Previously watched programs | Allowed, identically for every method |
+| Duplicate IDs within one ranking | Invalid in strict production evaluation |
+| Unknown/zero/malformed predicted IDs | Rejected in strict production evaluation |
+| Candidate availability | Positive-ID broadcasts overlapping the target period; schedule metadata only |
+| Cold-start fallback | Future training-only popularity ranking; interface and synthetic fixtures only in Step 3 |
+| Timezone | Europe/Kyiv-compatible clock, evidence-supported inference rather than an official rule |
+| Randomness | None in production evaluator/protocol construction; test seed 42 |
+
+**Do not compare one model's primary all-user MAP with another model's nonempty-only diagnostic.** Results returned by `EvaluationProtocol.evaluate` include the protocol ID, configuration hash, truth hash, cohort-order hash, and candidate-ID hash so later comparisons can identify a mismatched protocol.
+
+Machine-readable policy and source provenance are frozen in `data/step3/evaluation_config.json`, with its SHA-256 in `data/step3/evaluation_config.sha256`. The configuration includes the complete ordered cohort ID list, source roles, candidate restrictions/counts, the boundaries below, ground-truth rule, repeat/fallback rules, and file hashes.
+
+### Temporal boundaries
+
+| Role | Local half-open interval | UTC Unix-second interval |
+|---|---|---|
+| Hold-out training, Weeks 11–20 | `[2020-03-09 00:00, 2020-05-18 00:00)` | `[1583704800, 1589749200)` |
+| Validation, Weeks 21–30 | `[2020-05-18 00:00, 2020-07-27 00:00)` | `[1589749200, 1595797200)` |
+| Later final fitting only, Weeks 11–30 | `[2020-03-09 00:00, 2020-07-27 00:00)` | `[1583704800, 1595797200)` |
+| Later test availability, Weeks 31–42 | `[2020-07-27 00:00, 2020-10-19 00:00)` | `[1595797200, 1603054800)` |
+
+These match the verified Step 2 manifest. A recorded last-watch endpoint equal to a window's exclusive end is valid because it closes a half-open viewing interval; a first-watch timestamp at that end belongs to the next period. Step 3 does not parse user wall-clock timestamps again or reconstruct the join: it verifies the persisted UTC first/last timestamps and Step 2 provenance. Metadata-only candidate verification uses the established timezone interpretation and UTC elapsed broadcast durations.
+
 ## Inputs, schema inspection, and integrity
+
+### Actual input schema
+
+All three existing interaction files have the exact inspected header:
+
+```text
+user_id,tv_show_id,qualifying_airings,watched_seconds,first_watch_utc,last_watch_utc
+```
+
+Candidate files have `tv_show_id`; the cohort input has `user_id`. Headers, record widths, canonical numeric program IDs, exact string user IDs, sorted distinct user/program pairs, period membership, and minimum qualifying-duration consistency are validated. Unexpected records raise errors with source/row details instead of being silently dropped.
+
+For example, the first inspected training record is user `10008352999832730058`, program `20088`, nine qualifying airings and 8,581 seconds. Its first/last UTC endpoints are `1585032071` and `1589436000`. The history input has the same schema but is forbidden as hold-out training input; it was inspected and checked as an existing artifact only.
+
+### Input and output SHA-256 fingerprints
+
+Paths below are relative to `SWEETTV_Final_Exam/`:
+
+| File | SHA-256 |
+|---|---|
+| `data/step2/threshold_120s/train_interactions.csv.gz` | `3af4022f659c7c804ba791114963394b321baa813debe7aec6fac1b9947f1a93` |
+| `data/step2/threshold_120s/validation_interactions.csv.gz` | `e85ff75d56a13f44784ee8fa765e754050e3fc2e7719fcf6b627df16e4f62912` |
+| `data/step2/threshold_120s/history_interactions.csv.gz` | `7093e882ca1e1f9763340681b7f0009e32e9d2803be90513c68c6dcd8fb01834` |
+| `data/step2/train_candidates.csv` | `93ec316b22aa0d2791f3393dc984ec6262c66f3b92e75ea3466d5867119b0470` |
+| `data/step2/validation_candidates.csv` | `6f6ae055d0af1a70aa4e1b691cbc12cd054f2b80679643351e81dd8bcf22cd19` |
+| `data/step2/test_candidates.csv` | `28fc2ed785ab57cb70e90609e0edd4e9c18b9268f1794212356b9883a2112bfa` |
+| `data/step2/template_users.csv` | `5192399554230bf4feee964b0c55e29ed12117e50170272a052b49a3c59e9c61` |
+| `data/step2/join_manifest.json` | `3758a9c343afc6a67f9bf1b17d61714f820fc22dc614b392e7def06aae379df3` |
+| `data/step2/threshold_120s/interaction_manifest.json` | `8795ccb204122b4694fd18c7934fd0fec972d9487223e502476e7e4d75af3c87` |
